items.title: D.R. Horton's CEO says the giant homebuilder isn't betting on lower mortgage rates in 2027
items.description: Today’s letter is brought to you by Prophetic ! Land acquisition still runs on spreadsheets, cold calls, and gut instinct. Prophetic gives homebuilders and land teams one AI-native platform for sourcing, feasibility, and outreach, with every deal tracked in a single pipeline. It also surfaces off-market land before it's ever listed, so you can find sites your competitors don't even know exist. Teams on Prophetic move faster from first look to signed contract, so the best parcels don't end up in someone else's pipeline. Curious what that looks like on your own market? See it in action. D.R. Horton closed out fiscal 2026 with around 84,000 homes closed—roughly in line with the reduced guidance it issued last quarter. For fiscal 2027, D.R. Horton guided to 79,000 to 84,000 homes closed—wider ranges than usual, given the uncertainty. The message from management: the nationally aggregated housing market remains soft heading into 2027. During their last earnings call, D.R. Horton’s management said that guidance assumes mortgage rates stay around the recent range. Any sales upside on performance next year, in D.R. Horton’s view, is more likely to come from improving consumer sentiment—a calmer geopolitical backdrop, lower gas prices—than a material decline in long-term interest rates/mortgage rates. Executives described today's buyers as interested but cautious and tentative, held back by affordability and negative headlines. [ ResiClub members can read our 12-chart deep dive on D.R. Horton here ] "I think that anticipating [mortgage rates] to go down isn't prudent at all. So as we look at our guide for the year [we] expect that we're going to continue to see elevated rates. We'll see how that progresses through the spring… and what happens with consumer confidence. If we see some stability in the geopolitical environment, we see some reduction in gas prices and some other things that bring that back, we think that'll help with the market, but [we're] not expecting to see much reduction in rates in the near term." Right now, most economic models (and forward-looking market bets) don’t expect a significant short-term decline in mortgage rates unless something material shifts in the economy (e.g., a spike in the unemployment rate or the AI buildout losing momentum). Fannie Mae’s latest forecast projects the 30-year fixed mortgage rate to average 7.20% in Q4 2027 . Wells Fargo’s latest outlook similarly sees the 30-year fixed mortgage rate averaging 6.85% in Q4 2027 . The Mortgage Bankers Association forecast the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate to average 7.10% in Q4 2027 . Keep in mind that forecasts for long-term yields—including mortgage rates—shouldn’t be taken as guaranteed given nailing them also takes getting so much right about the underlying U.S. economy. There’s a lot that goes into financial markets pricing long-term yields/mortgage rates —and if the broader macro picture shifts, so can long-term yields/mortgage rates. Another thing to keep in mind is that even if these forecasts come fairly close to reality, weekly average 30-year fixed mortgage rate readings could still swing above or below the quarterly projected averages. After all, a ResiClub analysis of Freddie Mac’s weekly mortgage rate dataset (see above) finds that since 1972, the average annual range in the 30-year fixed mortgage rate has been 1.40 percentage points (140 bps). Narrowing the window to this century (since 2001), the average annual range has been 1.08 percentage points. In 2025, the spread between the year's highest and lowest weekly readings was 0.87 percentage points (87 basis points). In 2026 (not included in the table above because the year isn't over yet), the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate in Freddie Mac's weekly series has ranged 142 basis points, from a low of 5.98% to a high of 7.40%. Homeownership comes with a lot of responsibility that renters never had to think about. For many Gen Z and millennial buyers, that's a real barrier. "1 in 10 millennials actually doesn't know the difference between a flathead and Phillips screwdriver," Paul Koop , CEO of Builder Backed, said at ResiDay 2026 in New York City earlier this month. Builder Backed is trying to close that gap. The Cincinnati-based company partners directly with homebuilders to act as a concierge after closing. It uses each home's plot plans, blueprints, and HOA documents so owners can get quotes from local contractors and pay for the work inside their builder's app. Owners use it for first-year customizations like fences, blinds, and wainscoting, and for ongoing maintenance like HVAC and lawn care. The service stays with the house. Builder Backed spent the past few years developing the model with Fischer Homes—America’s 32nd largest homebuilder. Fischer's sales teams have pointed to specific deals where it helped them win over buyers choosing between builders. Up to 30% of Fischer homeowners have opted in, and the company is aiming for more than 50%. Koop also said Builder Backed is now ready to expand to other builders and can launch in a new market in under 30 days. Koop thinks builders can eventually follow the auto industry's Lexus playbook: build the home, service it, and resell it under a brand buyers recognize. Forward BTR List to clients and colleagues. They can sign up here . DISPOSITION: Pure Cycle plans to sell 51-home SFR portfolio near Denver. Pure Cycle's board has decided to stop investing in new rental homes and to sell its single-family rental portfolio at Sky Ranch, its master-planned community east of Denver, according to its latest 10-K filing. The company owns 51 rental homes there, about 98% occupied, with a carrying value of $18.3M, and plans to sell them one at a time as leases expire, offering tenants the chance to buy. DEVELOPMENT: Center Park starts site work on 79 BTR townhomes in Wilmington. Center Park Group has started site development on a 79-townhome build-to-rent community on about 11 acres in Wilmington, NC, in continued collaboration with Canvas Residential Partners. The site sits along North Kerr Avenue, just south of Martin Luther King Jr. Parkway and next to Azalea Landing. FUNDRAISING: Capital Square fills $24.06M offering for 238-home BTR near Phoenix. Capital Square has fully subscribed a $24.06M offering backed by a 238-home build-to-rent community under construction in Buckeye, AZ, which it is co-developing with Sunstone Two Tree. Founder and co-CEO Louis Rogers said BFR residents, often families with children and pets, tend to stay longer, which lowers turnover costs, and co-CEO Whitson Huffman said employers, health systems and retailers keep investing in the area. Capital Square has launched 17 BTR offerings totaling 1,814 homes in seven states. MARKET: NAHB: BTR starts hold at 69,000 over the past four quarters. BTR now makes up just over 7% of all single-family starts, compared with a 1992–2012 average of 2.7%. NAHB's Robert Dietz noted that the count leaves out homes sold to other parties for rental use, which could add another 3% to 5% of single-family starts. items.title: Blatstein Lines Up Refi Of North Philly Shopping Center After Loan Maturity
items.description: The financing underpinning a North Philadelphia shopping center undergoing a partial residential conversion is up in the air, but the borrower said there will be more certainty soon. Google Maps The Shops at Avenue North The $27M loan for The Shops at Avenue North, just south of Temple University ’s main campus, has been transferred to special servicing after it matured last month, according to Morningstar Credit . The 94K SF property at 1600 N. Broad St., 40% of which is occupied by an AMC Theatres location, is owned by Tower Investments . “It’s being refinanced before the end of the year,” Tower CEO Bart Blatstein told Bisnow on Wednesday. “The payoff statement was requested a while back” The borrower has been working on a refinancing since July as the maturity approached, but there was still no term sheet as of Oct. 13, according to commentary from special servicer Rialto Capital Advisors . Blatstein declined Bisnow ’s request for more details about the upcoming refinancing deal. Occupancy at the shopping center was 100% when Deutsche Bank originated the loan in 2018. Temple used to lease space at the property for a gym, but it has since departed. The owner is working to convert that section of the building into 24 studio apartments set to deliver before the start of the upcoming school year in August 2027, Blatstein said. Enrollment at Temple fell by 26% to just under 30,000 students between 2017 and last year, according to the university . Greater Philadelphia's retail market has shown signs of strength: It had a vacancy rate of 4.5% last quarter, down 10 basis points year-over-year, according to a report from Marcus & Millichap . Asking rents grew 2.9% over the same period and are expected to reach $21.10 per SF by the end of the year, following declines in 2024 and 2025. The Shops at Avenue North isn't the only property where Blatstein is in the midst of financial maneuvering. His Showboat Hotel in Atlantic City is facing potential foreclosure proceedings over a pair of CMBS loans totaling approximately $48M. Investors in June sought a court-ordered sheriff’s sale to satisfy the unpaid balance on the loans, the Philadelphia Business Journal reported . Last month, Blatstein proposed taking out a $21.5M personal loan in an effort to resolve the matter. items.title: Investors Face Total Loss On Portland Hilton Hotels With 83% Value Drop
items.description: The holders of bonds backing two Hilton hotels in downtown Portland, Oregon, are expected to face a complete loss after the properties’ valuation plummeted. Google Maps The Hilton Portland Downtown The Hilton Portland Downtown and the Duniway Portland, which sit just steps away from each other and total 782 rooms, have a new appraisal of $58M, Morningstar Credit reported last month. That appraisal, completed in July, represents an 83% drop from their $340.3M valuation seven years prior, when a note to refinance the properties was packaged into a commercial mortgage-backed security, Bloomberg reported this week. The new appraisal means that the value placed on these assets is less than a quarter of the $240M in debt on them. Meanwhile, $53M in advances have been executed to cover costs associated with the properties, meaning that any sale at the current valuation would result in a total loss for bondholders, according to Bloomberg. Such a sale is not imminent, according to special servicer commentary from SitusAMC Holdings Corp. filed with Morningstar Credit, with marketing “on hold pending an improvement of the market.” “The Portland hospitality market is distressed,” the commentary noted. It notes that the February sale of the Portland Marriott for $30M — a 63% discount from its 2013 price — was the city's first sale post-Covid. But a meeting with the Portland travel bureau signaled “green shoots for increased demand” coming to the city in 2027 and 2028, SitusAMC wrote. The Hilton Portland Downtown and the Duniway Portland were formerly owned by affiliates of Brookfield Asset Management , which purchased them in 2015 for $270M, according to Bloomberg. The affiliates refinanced the loan in 2019 when they were repackaged as a CMBS. But in 2020, BAM's affiliates defaulted on their mortgage, and in 2023, the properties were foreclosed on, leaving them in the hands of the bondholders. Brookfield spent $36.6M on renovations to the properties following its acquisition, according to Bloomberg, citing the bond's prospectus. During the first half of the year, the Portland hotels had a negative net operating income of $410K, according to Morningstar Credit. During that time, the properties made nearly as much in revenue as they spent in operating expenses: about $36M came in, while approximately just as much went out. That 100% operating expense ratio compares to a 90% ratio for all of 2025 and 80% during both of the prior years. items.title: Freddie Mac: AI investment Volatility Prompts Rates to Pull Back
items.description: Freddie Mac: AI investment Volatility Prompts Rates to Pull Back By Danielle Hale Nov 25, 2026 What happened to mortgage rates this week? The Freddie Mac 30-year fixed mortgage rate pulled back 7 basis points this week to 7.21%, recovering some of the previous-week’s jump that brought rates to 7.28%, as the 10-year Treasury yield has fallen back below 5%. The AI investment trade has created volatility in financial markets as investors try to value companies amid a whiplash-inducing news cycle that included, among other topics, the Anthropic IPO which gave the company a valuation greater than every home currently listed for sale . We’ve already seen AI-generated wealth shape consumer housing behavior, via higher down payments higher in the San Francisco Bay area and other tech hubs . Inflation continues to exceed the Fed’s target raising expectations for a December Fed rate hike, placing a floor under interest rates, including mortgage rates. The October CPI report was higher than expected . Today’s PCE reading reinforced that both overall (+3.8%) and core inflation (+3.3%), which excludes more volatile food and energy prices, continue to be too high; both measures edged up in October from September. The debate is not whether the Fed hikes in December, but how aggressively it moves. What does this mean for the housing market? Despite this week’s decline, mortgage rates remain roughly a percentage point above where they were at this point in 2025, adding another headwind for buyers contending with high home prices. Amid a challenging environment, it’s not surprising that a record high number of young adults are still living with their parents , but digging in below the national headline reveals noteworthy regional trends. Young adults in the Northeast are more likely to live at home than their peers in the West, South, or Midwest . However, a recent increase in multi-family supply has enabled an improvement in the Northeast, even as co-residence among young adults in other regions continued to climb.

items.title: New Home Sales Rebound in October due to Strong Performance in the South
items.description: New Home Sales Rebound in October due to Strong Performance in the South By Joel Berner Nov 25, 2026 October 2026 New-Home Sales What happened this month New home sales picked up in October to a seasonally adjusted annual pace of 701,000. This is a 14.2% increase from September and a 7.5% increase from last October. This is the highest monthly sales pace of 2026 so far, but year-to-date new home sales remain 3.0% below last year’s level as sales have been weak for most of the year. The median new home sales price continues to fall, this month’s level of $392,600 is 0.3% below last month’s price and 3.2% below last year’s. Builders are lowering prices to meet demand, and the median new home sales price remains well below the median existing home sales price . Regionally, the only gains were in the South, which saw a 36.2% increase from last month and a 24.7% increase from October 2025. As the largest region for new home sales, the South’s strong performance was enough to pull the national figure into positive territory. The Northeast posted a significant pullback, down 40.0% month over month and 63.4% year over year, but this data is often noisy as Northeast sales only make up about 4.2% of actual sales year-to-date. The Midwest fell 9.4% month over month and 10.5% year over year, while the West fell 25.4% month over month and 16.1% year over year. Inventory growth has slowed The increased pace of sales pulled the months’ supply down to 8.0, its lowest mark of the year. The market remains in buyer’s territory, but the decreased inventory (down 1.5% month over month and 4.1% year over year) is moving it back toward balance. That inventory continues to contain an elevated share of homes that have not yet started construction, higher than the share of completed new homes for sale. Builders are exercising caution, preferring to line up a buyer for their homes before starting work on them rather than building as many spec homes. New construction remains a strong alternative to the existing home segment, offering savings on mortgage rates , sale prices, and total cost of ownership .

items.title: Weekly Housing Trends: U.S. Market Update (Week Ending Nov. 21, 2026)
items.description: Weekly Housing Trends: U.S. Market Update (Week Ending Nov. 21, 2026) By Jake Krimmel Nov 25, 2026 Welcome to this weekly housing trends update, where we bring you the latest snapshot of inventory trends, listing activity, and buyer-seller dynamics across the U.S. housing market. In addition to our monthly housing trends reports , which offer deeper insights into long-term patterns, we publish these weekly updates to provide more timely views into market changes. This effort began in response to rapid shifts in the economy and housing landscape. You can count on a new Weekly Housing Trends update, fresh weekly data each Thursday, and a weekly video from our economists to help you stay informed. What this week's data shows Mortgage rates surged 18 basis points last week to 7.28%, and the housing market is feeling it. Active inventory is up 9.4% from a year ago, the highest weekly growth since January, even though sellers are listing fewer homes than last year. Homes are taking 2 days longer to sell for a second straight week, and the median listing price has fallen to its lowest level since early February. The affordability squeeze reaches beyond the buyers sitting out the market. Our new analysis shows a record 25.2 million adults under 35 living with their parents , a sign that the cost of housing is preventing new household formation. For buyers who can act, fewer shoppers means less competition, more homes to choose from, and sellers who are more open to negotiating. Active inventory climbed 9.4% year-over-year The number of homes for sale rose 9.4% compared to a year ago, up from last week's 8.6% and the highest weekly growth since January. It is also the fifth straight week of growth at 8% or higher, and growth has climbed from roughly 2% in mid-July. Active listings eased slightly from last week to 1.157 million, but that decline is smaller than the one a year ago, which is why the annual gap keeps widening. With new listings running below last year, the build comes from unsold homes piling up as buyers hold back. Year-to-date, active inventory is up 5.2%. Homes spent 2 days longer on the market compared to a year ago Median days on market came in at 68 days, with homes selling 2 days slower than the same week last year for the second week in a row. That is the fifth straight week of slower sales and keeps the gap at its widest since mid-April, after a stretch from late May through mid-October when homes sold at the same pace or faster than last year. With rates jumping again, the pullback in buyer demand is unlikely to ease soon. Year-to-date, time on market remains 2 days slower. New listings, a measure of sellers putting homes up for sale, fell 5.0% year-over-year New listing activity fell 5.0% year over year, the eighth straight week of annual declines and a step back from last week's 3.5% drop. Over the past three weeks, new listings have averaged roughly 6% below last year's pace, as buyers stay disengaged and owners with low-rate mortgages have little reason to trade into a costlier loan. Year-to-date, new listings are down 0.6%. The median listing price fell 2.4% year-over-year The median listing price was $400,000, down 2.4% from the same week last year and the lowest level since early February. Listing prices have now been negative on a year-over-year basis for 45 consecutive weeks. The median price per square foot fell 1.3% year over year, and year-to-date, median listing prices sit 1.9% below 2025 levels.

items.title: New home sales surge in October, but demand signals remain soft
items.description: New home sales blipped above expectations in October, handing homebuilders a slice of better-than-worse, Thanksgiving-time, good news. However, NAHB's November homebuilder confidence gauge had plunged to its lowest level in nearly 15 years, signaling that builders remain pessimistic about the market's current state and foreseeable-future direction. According to U.S. Census Bureau data, sales of newly constructed single-family homes in October came in at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 701,000, up 14.2% month-over month, and a 7.5% gain from the same month a year prior. Meanwhile, the median sales price of new homes sold in October was $391,000, down 0.3% from September and 3.2% from a year ago. October's better-than-forecast results may surprise many, but they come with a catch: the survey's margin of error and data collection cycle. They could be revised downward next month. “A downward revision to September helps explain the size of October’s 14.2% rebound, the largest monthly gain since November 2025,” First American Deputy Chief Economist Odeta Kushi said in a statement. New home for-sale inventory also tightened, coinciding with a decline in new residential construction . The seasonally adjusted estimate of new homes for sale at the end of October was 470,000, down 1.5% from September's 477,000, and 4.1% below the 490,000 recorded in October 2025. At the current sales rate, that represents a supply of 8.0 months, a 14% improvement from 9.3 months in September and 11.1% from 9.0 months a year earlier. October's sales results may be less of a bright spot than they appear, and one strong month doesn't erase the warning signs flashing across the new home market. Warning signs flash Plenty of indications suggest homebuilders are working through one of the toughest housing markets in years, including homebuilder confidence at its lowest point since the tail end of the Great Financial Crisis. For example, mortgage applications for new-home purchases fell 13.6% year over year in October, a sign that rising mortgage rates and low consumer confidence continue to weigh on demand. The existing-home market is also struggling, with the National Association of Realtors reporting that pending home sales fell to another record low in October. NAHB also reports that, in November, homebuilders had a bleak view of current sales conditions, future sales expectations for the next six months and prospective buyer traffic. "Persistent housing affordability challenges, including elevated home prices and mortgage rates, continue to weigh on prospective buyers and constrain demand," Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington, NAHB Assistant VP for Forecasting and Analysis, wrote in a note following today's new home sales release. "Builders are using sales incentives and price adjustments to attract buyers, but affordability remains a significant obstacle to a sustained recovery in housing demand." A review of the latest earnings calls from 14 publicly traded homebuilders reveals that the country's largest builders faced a challenging third quarter, with sales conditions remaining weak heading into the final months of the year, consistent with NAHB’s data. Last quarter, only three of the public homebuilders — Smith Douglas Homes , Toll Brothers and Green Brick Partners — reported year-over-year increases in new orders. However, nearly all 14 experienced sequential declines in orders, many exceeding 20%, pointing to a further deterioration in demand. Sales volume followed a similar trend. Only Smith Douglas Homes and LGI Homes reported year-over-year increases in homes sold, Meanwhile, just two builders, Toll Brothers (2.4%) and Hovnanian Enterprises (0.4%), posted year-over-year increases in average sales prices. Toll's luxury-focused buyer base is generally less sensitive to mortgage rates and economic volatility, while Hovnanian has increasingly shifted its product mix toward move-up and active-adult buyers, who tend to be more resilient to broader market pressures. Many public homebuilders reported in October and November that buyers remain very cautious, which helped dampen sales volume and prices. “As we moved through the quarter, our buyers became more cautious, did not feel an urgency to transact and felt more comfortable moving to the sidelines,” Century Communities Executive Chairman Dale Francescon said during an earnings call on October 28. Paul Romanowski, President and CEO at D.R. Horton , acknowledged that October was another challenging month. “Demand did get weaker as the quarter went on, for sure. As rates rose and as we got into October, what we've seen mirrors September. Traffic and sales activity are somewhat below what we'd anticipate in a typical seasonal pattern,” he said during an earnings call on October 29. Against this backdrop, it remains unclear whether October's sales rebound reflects a meaningful improvement in demand or a temporary spike that could show up next month as a downward revision. “Looking ahead, the question is whether enough buyers will follow those who signed contracts in October,” Kushi said, pointing to falling mortgage applications for new homes and low homebuilder confidence. “Builders are finding ways to make the monthly payment work for some buyers, but softer buyer traffic and fewer mortgage applications point to a tough winter.” Related More: Homebuilders New Home Sales U.S. Census Bureau

The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). Changes in Information Shared In 1984 , the 1-year ARM was added to the survey. In 1991 , the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was added. In January 2005 , a 5/1 hybrid ARM series was added. items.title: New Home Sales Increase in October, but Remain Below Last Year's Pace
items.description: New Home Sales Increase in October, but Remain Below Last Year's Pace November 25, 2026 Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington No Comments Despite the monthly gain, new home sales continued to trail 2025 levels, with year-to-date sales through October down 3.0% compared to the same period last year. Persistent housing affordability challenges, including elevated home prices and mortgage rates , continue to weigh on prospective buyers and constrain demand. Builders are using sales incentives and price adjustments to attract buyers, but affordability remains a significant obstacle to a sustained recovery in housing demand. Sales of newly built single-family homes increased 14.2% in October to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 701,000, following a downwardly revised September estimate, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development and the U.S. Census Bureau . This represented a 7.5% increase from a year earlier. While the monthly increase is encouraging, the 3.0% year-to-date decline highlights the importance of looking beyond month-to-month fluctuations, as the broader trend continues to reflect softness in new home sales activity. A new home sale is recorded when a contract is signed, or a deposit is accepted, regardless of the stage of construction. The seasonally adjusted annual rate reflects the pace of sales that would occur over a 12-month period if current conditions persist. New single-family home inventory in October was at 470,000 units and was down 4.1% from a year ago. At the current sales pace, the months’ supply of new homes stood at an elevated 8.0 months, lower than 9.0 months' supply from a year ago. A five- to six-month inventory level generally indicates a balanced market. Combined new and existing home inventory has edged higher in recent months, with the total months’ supply reaching 5.4 months. Inventory conditions in the existing home market have gradually improved in recent months. Moderating prices across both markets have helped support buyer demand amid ongoing affordability concerns. At the end of October, there were 114,000 completed, ready-to-occupy homes available for sale on a non-seasonally adjusted basis. Completed homes accounted for approximately one-quarter of total inventory, while homes under construction made up 51%. The remaining share of homes sold in October had not yet started construction at the time the sales contract was signed. New home prices showed improvement in October, reflecting the use of builder incentives. The median new home sale price was $391,300, down 0.3% from September and down 3.2% compared to a year ago. Homes priced between $300,000 and $499,999 accounted for 46% of all new home sales, while one-quarter of sales were priced below $300,000, underscoring ongoing affordability challenges for entry-level buyers. The remaining 27% of sales were priced above $500,000. It is worth noting that the share of homes priced below $300,000 has increased since the beginning of the year, while the share priced over $500,000 has decreased. Regional performance was mixed in October. The South, the only region to post an increase, was up 36.2% from September. Sales were down 9.4% in the Midwest, 25.4% in the West, and 40.0% in the Northeast on a monthly basis. Compared with October 2025, the South recorded a 24.7% increase in new home sales, the only region to post an increase. Sales declined 10.5% in the Midwest, 16.1% in the West, and 63.4% in the Northeast. On a year-to-date basis, regional trends were similarly uneven. New home sales increased 0.1% in the South. items.description: Mortgage Rates Improve Again as Stock Slide Continues By: Matthew Graham 2 Hours, 14 Min ago As we discussed in greater detail yesterday, there's not a reliable rule for how stocks and interest rates correlate, but lately, lower stock prices have helped facilitate lower rates. That phenomenon proved out this morning as overnight stock losses helped the bond market open in much stronger territory (and stronger bonds = lower rates). Stocks ended up bouncing fairly decently in the early afternoon, but rates were less inclined to follow. We're not reading much into the weaker afternoon correlation simply due to the fact that the day before Thanksgiving often sees random volatility driven by a rush for the exits among traders. By remaining in stronger territory, the bond market allowed mortgage lenders to set rates at another 2-week low with the top-tier 30yr fixed rate now down to 7.26% from 7.32% yesterday. items.title: Apartment sales plummeted 43% in October
items.description: Apartment sales plummeted 43% in October Values dropped 6.3% YOY during the month, though MSCI suggests price declines may be easing. Published Nov. 25, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images Dive Brief: After the massive AvalonBay Communities-Equity Residential merger boosted apartment sales in the third quarter, the market came tumbling back to earth in October. Transactions plummeted 43% year over year to $7.6 billion, according to a report that data firm MSCI Real Assets shared with Multifamily Dive. This was the slowest October since 2012, when the industry was still digging out of the global financial crisis. It was also the second straight month of double-digit sales declines, according to MSCI. Still, apartment volume is up 51% year-to-date, driven by the Vivmark deal. Prices also fell in October, dropping 6.3% YOY, which was the steepest annual fall since June 2024. However, the annualized one-month change was -6.4%, which was the smallest decline since Q1 2026 and suggests price declines may be easing, according to MSCI. Dive Insight: Single asset sales fell 43% YOY to $6.8 billion in October, and entity trades dropped 40% YOY to $800 million. “While volume will likely revise upwards, this was a particularly difficult start to the fourth quarter,” MSCI wrote in the report. Garden property transactions and mid- and high-rise sales both totaled $3.8 billion in transactions during the month. For garden properties, that sum marked a 51% decline YOY, and for mid- and high-rise assets, a 31% decline. The apartment sector's $7.6 billion in sales trailed industrial’s $9.3 billion in October, according to a separate MSCI report. Office at $6.5 billion was followed by retail at $6 billion and hotel at $2.9 billion. Retail was the only segment to post a YOY October increase, up 5%. Apartment industry executives blame the increase in the 10-year Treasury for the slowdown in sales throughout 2026. In November 2025, it fell below 4% before eventually rising to more than 5.25% in October 2026, according to CNBC. As that happened, deals were shuttered across multifamily and the broader commercial real estate market. “We've seen the volatility and the increase in Treasuries, which has resulted in these higher financing costs and has created a lot of disruption in the market,” Lili Dunn, CEO and president of Bell Partners, told Multifamily Dive. “So as a result, volume has paused significantly.” If rates remain volatile, Dunn said, well-capitalized owners will wait for stability rather than sell at a discount. However, she is optimistic that deals will ultimately pick up in 2027. “I would say it will be gradual, not a surge,” Dunn said. “There seems to be a good amount of capital ready to invest, and fundamentals are actually attractive.” Click here to sign up to receive multifamily and apartment news like this article in your inbox every weekday. items.description: Agencies announce dollar thresholds for smaller loan exemption from appraisal requirements for higher-priced mortgage loans Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Federal Reserve Board Office of the Comptroller of the Currency For release at 3:00 p.m. EST Share --> --> --> --> --> --> The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Federal Reserve Board, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency today announced that the 2027 threshold for higher-priced mortgage loans that are subject to special appraisal requirements will increase from $34,200 to $35,500. The threshold amount will be effective January 1, 2027, and is based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W, as of June 1, 2026. The Dodd-Frank Act added special appraisal requirements for higher-priced mortgage loans to the Truth in Lending Act, including that creditors obtain a written appraisal based on a physical visit to the interior of the home before making a higher-priced mortgage loan. The rules implementing these requirements contain an exemption for loans at or below a threshold amount that is adjusted annually to reflect CPI-W increases. items.description: Texas could overtake California as one of the top international homebuying destinations as soon as 2027 by Emily Marek November 25, 2026 Texas made up 10.4% of international homebuyer demand in the third quarter of 2026, Realtor.com said. Dallas and Houston made up 3% and 2.4%, respectively. Texas is the third-most popular state for potential international homebuyers — but that could change as soon as next year if current trends continue, according to a new report from Realtor.com . The real estate site analyzed traffic from international countries in the third quarter to determine the states where non-United States residents are most interested in purchasing homes. Florida was the post popular destination for prospective buyers outside the country, making up 21.9% of all international searches; California followed at 10.8%, with Texas close behind at 10.4%. Dallas and Houston made up 3% and 2.4%, respectively. In comparison, California made up 14.2% of international traffic in the third quarter of 2019, while Texas has gained international interest annually since 2022. If current trends continue, Texas could make up its 0.5-point deficit as soon as 2027, Realtor.com said. “International home-shopping patterns are shifting, and Texas is moving closer to California as a destination for shoppers around the world,” Jiayi Xu , senior economist at Realtor.com, said in a press release. “At the same time, Canadians are making up a larger share of international interest again, and they’re already giving Texas a slight edge over California.” Canadians made up 35.9% of all international home interest in the U.S. — the largest share of any country, up from 32.3% a year prior. While that’s still down from Canada’s U.S. home interest levels in 2023 and 2024, it represents a meaningful increase from the past several years. Texas made up 8.8% of that traffic, compared to 8.6% for California. “Canadian shoppers are reinforcing their place in the international home-search picture after last year’s pullback,” Xu added. “Their interest spans familiar destinations like Florida and growing ones like Texas, but it also reaches northern and mountain states. That breadth is a reminder that international interest isn’t concentrated in just a handful of markets.” Overall, North American buyers outside the U.S. accounted for 47.7% of international interest, up 5% year over year, while European interest decreased to 2.45%, its lowest level since the third quarter of 2019. Despite decreasing interest in U.S. real estate overall, European searches for Texas homes have increased over the past several years: Texas accounted for 8% of European traffic, up from 7.1% in the third quarter of 2019. items.title: Case-Shiller: Miami home-price growth jumps in September
items.description: Case-Shiller: Miami home-price growth jumps in September by John Yellig November 24, 2026 The overall pace of home-price growth across the United States continued to increase on an annual basis in September despite large market variations: Chicago led the nation for the sixth month in a row, while Seattle remained in last place. The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price NSA Index rose 2.1% year over year in September, the same increase posted in August. Month over month, the index slipped 0.3%. S&P Dow Jones noted that home values actually fell in real terms for the 16th month in a row, as September's 3.7% inflation erased the 2.1% gain in prices. "Nominal home prices remain resilient, but inflation is once again widening the gap between nominal and real housing returns," said Rebecca Kaufman, associate director of commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices. "Consumer prices rose 3.7% year over year in September, accelerating from 3.4% in August, marking the 16th consecutive month in which U.S. home prices declined in real terms." In Miami, home prices jumped 4.6% year over year and 0.2% month over month in September. "Chicago led all metros for the sixth consecutive month, posting a 6.9% annual gain, followed by New York at 5.8% and Miami at 4.6%. Seattle recorded the largest annual decline for the fourth consecutive month at 1.9%, followed by Denver (-1.0%) and Dallas (-0.9%)," Kaufman said. " Miami's rise is particularly notable: After moving into fourth place among the 20 cities in July and August, it has now climbed into the top three, a sharp reversal from its comparatively weak performance in 2025." items.title: Arizona Department of Real Estate withdraws ERAS policy following legal action
items.description: Arizona Department of Real Estate withdraws ERAS policy following legal action by Emily Marek November 25, 2026 The ERAS program was introduced as a preventative measure against deed fraud. However, Arizona REALTORS® and LTAA’s joint lawsuit, filed against the Arizona Department of Real Estate on Nov. 18, claimed the system actually increased the risk of wire fraud. The Arizona Department of Real Estate withdrew its Early Real Estate Sales Alert System (ERAS) rule following legal action from Arizona REALTORS® and the Land Title Association of Arizona. The rule — Substantive Policy Statement 2026.02 — previously required Arizona real estate agents to provide details about ERAS and document their clients’ decision, or lack thereof, to participate. Noncompliant agents risked fines of up to $10,000 per violation. The ERAS program, which sends alerts to registered Arizona property owners when pending sales are reported, was introduced as a preventative measure against deed fraud . However, Arizona REALTORS® and LTAA’s joint lawsuit, filed against the department on Nov. 18, claimed the system actually increased the risk of wire fraud. The associations also claimed that ADRE did not give appropriate notice before enacting the ERAS regulations on Nov. 1, failing to give their party the opportunity to voice opposition. “Thanks to the cooperation and prompt assistance of the Office of the Arizona Governor, that lawsuit has been favorably resolved,” Arizona REALTORS® said in a statement. “The SPS is therefore void, unenforceable, and there is no legal obligation for Realtors to discuss ERAS with their clients or have them make an election via an ERAS form.” Arizona REALTORS® cited the following qualms with ERAS: Given the voluntary nature of the program, criminals posing as property owners have no incentive to participate. The program doesn’t include a verification method for property owners. “Bad actors” could potentially use the system to access information about pending transactions. “The Arizona REALTORS® does not pursue litigation lightly. However, when Realtors are threatened with fines of up to $10,000 per violation and the possible revocation of their license for failing to use a form that promotes a deeply flawed and ineffective system such as ERAS, the association has a duty to act on its members’ behalf,” the association concluded. “The Arizona REALTORS® is pleased that the matter was resolved amicably with the cooperation of the Governor’s office and Realtors are now free from the obligations imposed by SPS 2026.02 while ERAS remains available on a truly voluntary basis.” Agents who wish to discuss ERAS with clients may still choose to do so. items.title: Housing data shocks to the upside: Will we get sub-7% rates for Christmas?
items.description: Thanksgiving week has been crazy so far, with a stock rally, stocks selling off, the 10-year yield dropping below 4.85%, tariffs being announced, inflation running hot , low jobless claims, strong GDP data and then — the housing data surprised to the upside! Let’s look at what's happening as mortgage rates have fallen a tad from recent highs. Purchase apps and weekly demand grows As we've discussed in the Housing Market Tracker articles over the past few weeks, our weekly pending sales data has stabilized and last week it grew a bit. The housing market took a shock when rates rose aggressively from under 7% in September to 7.61% in early October; that shock really impacted demand, but rates haven’t gone higher than that and have eased a bit since. Those lower rates stabilized demand in our weekly pending home sales data, which grew last week. Purchase application data , on the other hand, has moved more noticeably. This index can be very tricky at times because it’s a survey, but to see this growth without rates below 7% is a good sign of stabilization. Of course, the year-over-year purchase application data is still down big, but last year mortgage rates were roughly 1% lower at this time and we were heading toward a nine-month high in sales last December. New home sales beat estimates New home sales today beat estimates so much that my first inclination was not to believe it! I expect this number will be revised lower, but it's still a positive trend. New home sales are basically doing the same thing they have done for 10 years, outside the COVID sales burst. They don’t really go below 570,000, nor do they really break away from 730,000. We are stuck in this range, as the builders are still working in a sub-6 % mortgage market, and thus new home sales are still at 2019 levels. If existing home sales were operating at those levels it would amount to 1-1.3 million more existing home sales. However, the existing home market hasn’t had the luxury of sub-6 % mortgage rates. One positive note that isn’t getting a lot of play is that the builders are slowly moving their completed units of sale lower. If we want housing starts to ever grow again, this needs to happen and fortunately this number has been falling all year long. As I am writing this article, the 10-year yield is at 4.82%. If we want sub-7 % rates for Thanksgiving, Christmas, or New Year's — as I have written about for weeks — we need the 10-year yield at 4.85% and under. Now, if spreads just improve a little, then we get our sub-7 % mortgage rates for the holidays. It’s been a wild week, folks; enjoy the holiday! Related More:

items.title: Fed's Preferred Inflation Gauge Accelerated to Three-Year High
items.description: Fed's Preferred Inflation Gauge Accelerated to Three-Year High November 25, 2026 Fan-Yu Kuo No Comments The Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge accelerated to a three-year high in October, further adding pressure on the Fed to maintain its tightening stance. While consumer spending continued to grow, real (inflation-adjusted) spending was nearly unchanged, suggesting persistent inflation is eroding household purchasing power. The headline Personal Consumption Expenditure (PCE) Price Index increased 3.8% in October from a year ago, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis . The “core” PCE price index, which excludes food and energy, rose 3.3% over the past twelve months, the fastest pace since November 2023. Core PCE has remained at or above 3.0% since the start of the Iran conflict, suggesting broad-based inflation pressure beyond energy. Consumer spending rose 0.3% in October, while real spending, adjusted to remove inflation, remained unchanged. Meanwhile, personal income rose 0.7% in October. This growth was led by increases in compensation, government social benefits, and personal income receipts on assets. Real disposable income—income adjusted for taxes and inflation—rose 0.5%. On a year-over-year basis, personal income was 4.8% higher, and real (inflation-adjusted) disposable income was up 1.6%. With spending growth outpacing income growth, the personal saving rate edged up to 4.1% in October. items.title: 2026Q3 International Demand Report: Texas Closes In on California as a Top Destination for International Home Shoppers
items.description: 2026Q3 International Demand Report: Texas Closes In on California as a Top Destination for International Home Shoppers By Jiayi Xu Nov 25, 2026 Highlights In 2026Q3, international home shoppers made up 1.3% of online shopping demand. International shoppers flocked to Miami, FL (8.3% of international demand in the U.S.), followed by New York, NY (5.9%), and Los Angeles, CA (4.7%). Three states lead, with different stories. Florida (21.9%), California (10.8%) and Texas (10.4%) drew 43.1% of international traffic in 2026Q3. Florida is steady, California is slipping from 14.2% in 2019Q3, and Texas is only 0.5 points behind California. If the trend holds, Texas could overtake California as soon as next year Canada’s share rose. Canadian shoppers account for 35.9% of international traffic, up from 32.3% a year ago and close to the 2023 and 2024 levels (36.1% and 36.9%). North American shoppers (excluding the U.S.) overall make up 47.7%, up 5 points from last year. Europe is pulling back. Eu ropean shoppers’ share of international traffic stood at its lowest Q3 levels since 2019 (24.5%). Montana and Tennessee are gaining a bigger slice of traffic from every group. In 2026Q3, 1.3% of Realtor.com® online traffic came from international home shoppers, down slightly from 1.5% in 2025Q3 but similar to the 1.2% in 2019Q3, the pre-pandemic level. Florida leads, California fades, Texas rises In 2026Q3, The most popular three states among international home shoppers are Florida, California and Texas, which together account for 43.1% of international traffic, but each has a different story. Florida remains the top destination for international home shoppers, drawing 21.9% of all international traffic. Miami, Orlando and Tampa are its leading metros, accounting for 8.3%, 2.9% and 2.5% of U.S. international traffic, respectively. Its share peaked at 24.5% in 2022 and has since settled around 21-22%, close to its 2019 level of 20.8%. California has been losing ground. After spiking to 16.6% in 2020, its share has slipped to 10.8%, down from 14.2% in 2019. Los Angeles, Riverside and San Diego are its top metros for international shoppers, drawing 4.7%, 1.4% and 1.2% of U.S. international traffic, respectively. Texas is catching up. Its share has risen every year since 2022, from 8.8% to 10.3%, narrowing the gap with California from 5.7 points in 2019 to just 0.5 today. If the trend holds, it could overtake California as soon as next year. Dallas and Houston are the leading metros that attract international home shoppers in 2026Q3, drawing 3.0% and 2.4% of U.S. international traffic. A handful of smaller states are gaining share of international traffic from low starting points. Montana doubled its share from 0.6% in 2019Q3 to 1.2% in 2026Q3, and Idaho (0.4% to 0.7%) and Vermont (0.3% to 0.6%) show similar gains, with Alaska (0.3% to 0.5%) and West Virginia (0.2% to 0.4%) also trending up. Tennessee, from a larger base, climbed from 1.5% to 1.9%. These states are small, but their steady increases suggest growing interest in outdoor and rural markets. Canada’s share rises, with Montana and Tennessee gaining In 2026 Q3, North American shoppers (excluding the U.S.) were the largest source of international demand, accounting for 47.7% of international traffic, up 5.0 percentage points from 42.7% a year earlier. Canada drove most of that gain: Canadian home shoppers were the No. 1 individual source, at 35.9% of international traffic. After Canadian interest in U.S. real estate declined sharply in 2025 , with its share falling to 32.3% in 2025 Q3, the share moved back to 35.9% in 2026 Q3, close to its pre-tariff levels of 36.1% in 2023 and 36.9% in 2024. Florida, Texas and California are the top states for Canadian home shoppers, and Texas has already edged past California (8.8% vs. 8.6% in 2026 Q3), a crossover that hasn’t yet happened in overall international traffic. Canadians also favor northern and mountain states more than other international shoppers do. Montana drew 2.0% of Canadian traffic in 2026 Q3, up from 1.3% in 2019 Q3 and well above its 1.2% share of overall international traffic, while Idaho doubled from 0.5% to 1.0%. Tennessee also saw growing Canadian interest, rising from 1.3% to 2.0%. Among the most popular metros, Canadian buyers dominated international views in Sun Belt and Southwest metros. Cape Coral, FL, led with 65.9% of its international demand coming from Canada, followed by Naples, FL (65.4%), Phoenix, AZ (62.6%) and North Port, FL (61.4%). Notably, these same markets also posted the largest year-over-year growth in Canadian interest between 2025 Q3 and 2026 Q3, led by Cape Coral (+8.9 ppt), Riverside (+6.4 ppt), Naples (+5.4 ppt), and Dallas (+5.0 ppt). However, Canadians’ interest in Chicago, IL (-1.0 ppt), Las Vegas, NV (-1.0 ppt), New York, NY (-0.4 ppt) and San Francisco, CA (-0.1 ppt) declined year over year. European interest in U.S. homes is cooling Europe moved the other way. European shoppers’ share of international traffic stood at its lowest Q3 levels since 2019 (24.5%). The U.K. (6.2% of international traffic) and Germany (3.7%) remain among the top sources of interest in U.S. homes, but both are at their lowest Q3 levels since 2019. The decline coincides with weaker European travel to the U.S. , suggesting that European interest in U.S. homes may be cooling alongside interest in visiting. Even so, a growing share of European traffic is going to New York and Texas. In 2026 Q3, New York drew 8.1% of European traffic, up from 6.0% in 2019 Q3, and Texas drew 8.0%, up from 7.1% in 2019 Q3. In addition, smaller states are also gaining ground among European shoppers. Montana’s share among European traffic nearly doubled, from 0.5% in 2019 Q3 to 0.9% in 2026 Q3, and Tennessee’s rose from 1.7% to 2.0%. Methodology This report analyzes international views of for-sale listings on the U.S. Realtor.com marketplace from July to September 2026 and previous quarters, as noted above.

items.title: Colorado first responders can now get state home mortgage help
items.description: A borrower earning nearly $197,000 a year usually doesn't look like a typical candidate for state housing help. In Colorado, if that borrower is a firefighter, emergency medical technician or police officer, the person now qualifies. The Colorado Housing and Finance Authority launched a homeownership program this month for first responders and law enforcement officers. CHFA Colorado Champions uses a new state law that raises income limits for eligible borrowers. Colorado is among a growing list of states offering homebuying assistance to public-service workers. The goal is to give them more chances to live near where they serve. Maryland, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Texas, Florida and South Carolina also offer similar programs. Earlier this month, Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont announced a new homeownership assistance program for first responders. It offers up to $25,000 in forgivable down payment and closing cost assistance. The program stems from a law Lamont signed this year. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them,” Lamont said in a statement. State housing help arrives in a softening market CHFA Colorado Champions arrives as the housing market weakens, following several years of zoning and regulatory reform. Colorado's single-family housing market has been steadily cooling since spring, according to HousingWire Intelligence data through Nov. 20. Inventory peaked in September and has barely eased, while median list prices have fallen since July. Homes are also taking longer to sell, with days on market rising since late July and price reductions staying elevated. The latest weekly figures show no reversal, with single-family homes taking a median 91 days to sell, up from 84. The median single-family list price is $599,000, and about 48% of single-family listings carry price cuts, the data show. Lawmakers have spent years trying to improve affordability, mostly by loosening local land-use rules. In 2024, Gov. Jared Polis signed laws requiring more density near transit and clearing the way for accessory dwelling units. The package also removed some parking minimums for urban multifamily housing and lifted limits on unrelated people living together. A law Polis signed this year requires towns with more than 2,000 people to allow housing on certain small parcels. Eligible land belongs to school districts, colleges, transit districts, housing authorities and qualifying nonprofits. The law takes effect Dec. 31, 2027, while lot-size bills failed in the Legislature this year. How Colorado Champions works Senate Bill 26-053, a bipartisan law, raised CHFA's mortgage income limits to 110% of standard guidelines. That allows eligible borrowers earning up to $196,810 a year to qualify. The program offers a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage. The program covers down payment and closing costs up to the lesser of $25,000 or 4% of the first mortgage. Borrowers apply through a CHFA participating lender. The aid is a second mortgage. Repayment is deferred until the term ends, the first mortgage is paid off, or the borrower sells, refinances or moves. CHFA Executive Director Thomas Bryan said in a statement that first responders keep communities safe. Many can't afford local homes, he added. “They should be able to live where they serve,” Sen. Barbara Kirkmeyer, one of the law’s sponsors, said in a statement. Related More: Affordability mortgage

items.title: FHFA keeps loan caps unchanged at $176B in 2027
items.description: FHFA keeps loan caps unchanged at $176B in 2027 Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will each have an $88 billion multifamily limit, though workforce lending will be excluded from the caps. Published Nov. 25, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images Dive Brief: The Federal Housing Finance Agency kept the multifamily loan purchase caps unchanged at $88 billion each for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac for 2027 , giving them a combined limit of $176 billion next year, according to a Nov. 23 press release. FHFA will continue to require that at least 50% of the enterprises’ multifamily loan purchases be designated as mission-driven affordable housing, per the release. As it was in 2026, loans that ensure workforce housing will be excluded from the limits. The caps will continue to apply to other mission-driven loans. As in past years, FHFA “will continue to monitor the multifamily mortgage market and will increase the caps if necessary,” as it aims to “provide sufficient liquidity and support in the multifamily mortgage market,” according to the release. However, the caps will remain at $176 billion even if the market is smaller than expected. Dive Insight: Despite a slow sales market, multifamily executives said there were plentiful options in the lending market in 2026. Debt funds remained active and banks and insurers grew increasingly aggressive over the summer. Still, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac remain viable options for borrowers. “The primary agency execution [for us] is Fannie and Freddie, and then we have other strategic lenders that we were using as well,” Mike Ruiz, a partner in acquisitions and development with Carmel Partners, told Multifamily Dive. Jon Siegel, co-founder and chief investment officer of RailField Partners, said it will be interesting to see what next year looks like for the agencies, as demand increases to refinance loans. “We've all seen the numbers around maturities, which would make you think that there should be plenty of demand for financing, but a lot of those loans aren't going to underwrite for an agency execution today,” Siegel told Multifamily Dive in emailed comments. "If you have a five-year loan that is maturing, the increase in Treasuries coupled with the trajectory of NOI's [net operating income] over that period makes the math hard for a lot of borrowers.” Siegel expects transaction volume to remain down, limiting demand for acquisition financing. “Of course, the flip side is that the agencies have goals that they need to meet, and we will likely see them make adjustments to be more competitive without taking on greater risk,” Siegel said. “That combination is probably a good thing for borrowers that have more straightforward deals.” In 2025, FHFA established lending caps of $73 billion each for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, allowing them to purchase up to $146 billion in multifamily loans. In 2024, they were allotted $70 billion each , and in 2023, they were given $75 billion each. items.description: Agencies announce dollar thresholds for applicability of truth in lending and consumer leasing rules for consumer credit and lease transactions Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Federal Reserve Board For release at 3:00 p.m. EST Share --> --> --> --> --> --> The Federal Reserve Board and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau today announced the dollar thresholds used to determine whether certain consumer credit and lease transactions in 2027 are subject to certain protections under Regulation Z (Truth in Lending) and Regulation M (Consumer Leasing). By law, the agencies are required to adjust the thresholds annually based on the annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W. Transactions at or below the thresholds are subject to the protections of the regulations. Specifically, based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the CPI-W as of June 1, 2026, Regulation Z and Regulation M generally will apply to consumer credit transactions and consumer leases of $76,300 or less in 2027. However, private education loans and loans secured by real property, such as mortgages, are subject to Regulation Z regardless of the amount of the loan. items.description: Better Home & Finance Holding Co. signed an agreement with an unnamed mortgage servicer to offer home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and home equity loans to existing borrowers, expanding its lead-generation channels as the company continues its turnaround efforts. The agreement, announced Tuesday in the company's Week 7 Better 2.0 scorecard, is expected to provide a lower-cost customer acquisition channel. Since its Week 6 scorecard on Nov. 17, Better has identified additional efficiencies across its corporate organization that are expected to generate a total of $38.97 million in annualized savings. The company also reported $770,000 in additional annualized savings from mortgage operations. Better said it plans to pursue another $1.5 million in vendor-related reductions by Dec. 1. The company is working toward a broader cost savings target of $64.2 million. “ HELOC volume with our partners continues to grow each week, four more brokerages are lined up to join our wholesale platform, and two new partnerships are set to launch. At the same time, we're moving toward a signed agreement to sell Birmingham Bank , which will let us focus fully on our U.S. business,” said Vishal Garg , Better's founder and head of product, platform and innovation. The company has received five term sheets for about $50 million in debt financing tied to the proposed sale of the bank and is continuing discussions with prospective financing partners. The company said its AI-powered HELOC partnership with a large existing customer is live, with volume increasing weekly. Better is also preparing a multichannel campaign to expand the product through its wholesale platform and onboard additional brokerages. Four more mortgage brokerages are in the pipeline to join the platform. Two previously announced partnerships — with a rental credit management platform and a home inspection company — are expected to launch early next week. items.title: The Fed is likely to raise rates in December. What it means for your holiday spending
items.description: Read more CNBC personal finance coverage Trump Account contributions from friends and family pass $1 billion mark, Treasury says The Fed is likely to raise rates in December. What it means for your holiday spending Trump administration proposes rule that could curb ESG investing in 401(k)s CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 The central bank sets the federal funds rate, the interest rate at which banks borrow and lend to one another overnight. Although consumers do not pay that rate directly, changes to the federal funds rate ripple through many of the borrowing costs they face every day. When the Fed raises rates, borrowing becomes more expensive, helping to slow economic activity and ease inflation. But as a result, Americans may face higher costs for mortgages, auto loans and credit cards, among other forms of debt. Credit card rates will rise Pressmaster | Istock | Getty Images Credit cards are particularly sensitive to Fed policy because most carry variable interest rates. As the federal funds rate rises, so does the prime rate, which credit card issuers use as a benchmark. Card rates typically adjust within one or two billing cycles after the Fed adjusts its policy. That will come at a difficult time for consumers. Not only are Americans heading into the fourth quarter carrying a record $1.29 trillion in credit card debt, but 66% of consumers with unsecured debt are still paying off last year's holiday purchases, according to a recent survey of 2,000 U.S. adults by National Debt Relief, a debt settlement firm. "What's particularly concerning is that many Americans are heading into this holiday season still paying off debt from the last one," Peter Beaugard, chief revenue officer at National Debt Relief, said in a written statement. "When holiday spending turns into debt that carries over year after year, it can create a cycle that becomes increasingly difficult to break." With affordability already stretched , higher borrowing costs could put additional pressure on household budgets, though the impact is unlikely to be felt evenly, experts said. "Higher-income households that pay their card balance in full won't see any significant change in what ends up under the tree," said Cristian deRitis, deputy chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "Lower-income and younger households already leaning on credit cards will feel the pinch," he said. Higher interest rates are intended to cool demand. As borrowing becomes more expensive and debt burdens grow, households may have little choice but to pull back on spending in the months ahead, experts say. That may include holiday spending, though consumers may first opt to look for savings elsewhere, experts said. "Some spending will be trimmed, but consumers will likely cut elsewhere before they cut gifts," deRitis said. Car loans and mortgage rates remain elevated Other borrowing costs are affected more indirectly by the central bank. However, anyone shopping for a car or home this holiday season could still be impacted by the Fed's next move. Auto loan rates , for example, are tied to several factors, including the Fed's benchmark. Even as new-car APRs hover above 7% and car prices remain elevated, December is traditionally a good time to buy a vehicle as dealers look to clear inventory before the end of the year, according to Ivan Drury, director of insights at Edmunds. "Normally, waiting for December APR deals comes with a tradeoff: shrinking inventory of current-model-year vehicles, where discounts would provide the most value," he said. This year, however, buyers face an added hurdle. Auto loan interest rates remain near historic highs — and could go even higher — while the average transaction price has climbed above $50,000. A home for sale in Los Angeles, California, Nov. 20, 2026. Justin Sullivan | Getty Images Alternatively, 15- and 30-year fixed mortgage rates don't move with the Fed's benchmark rate. Instead, they generally track long-term Treasury yields , which remain elevated. As a result, 30-year fixed mortgage rates have stayed above 7% since September, according to Mortgage News Daily , pushing the real estate sector into a deep freeze . watch now VIDEO 2:52 02:52 Frozen market hits homebuyers The Exchange "Now that we're entering the holiday season, many buyers who were hoping to be in a new home for the holidays may still find themselves in wait-and-see mode, hoping mortgage rates eventually move back into the 6% range," said Jeff DerGurahian, chief investment officer and head economist at loanDepot. However, mortgage rates won't automatically move higher if the Fed raises its benchmark interest rate, DerGurahian said. For example, if the central bank's move aligns with market expectations and signals that inflation is moving in the right direction, Treasury yields could fall — and mortgage rates could benefit, he said. "However, if Fed officials suggest more aggressive tightening still lies ahead, Treasury yields and mortgage rates could face renewed pressure," he said. "And while a hike may not be the holiday gift borrowers were hoping for, there is still a path for mortgage rates to move into the high 6% range before we ring in the new year." items.description: Vornado Realty Trust has agreed to sell a 49% stake in 90 Park Ave . in a deal that values that office tower at $722.5M, or $755 per SF. San Francisco-based investment firms Sixth Street Partners and DivcoWest are buying into the 956K SF building, which takes up the full western blockfront of Park Avenue at East 40th Street. Vornado Realty Trust The nearly 1M SF office tower at 90 Park Ave. Vornado will retain a majority interest in the property and continue to oversee management and leasing. The property is unencumbered, but the newly formed joint venture plans to obtain a nonrecourse loan of at least $500M tied to the asset. Vornado expects to receive net proceeds of approximately $575M from the transaction, the REIT announced in a press release Tuesday. The deal is expected to close by the end of the year. Newmark 's Adam Spies , Josh King and Adam Doneger represented Sixth Street Partners, while Eastdil Secured Savills ' Gary Phillips and Will Silverman represented Vornado. The office portion of the tower is fully leased, according to Vornado’s third-quarter earnings report . However, Alston & Bird, which occupies approximately 123K SF across multiple floors, inked a lease earlier this year to relocate to 170K SF at Harbor Group International ’s 51 W. 52nd St. Finding a replacement is unlikely to be an issue. Grand Central’s vacancy rate is among the lowest in the city, at 16.6%, according to Cushman & Wakefield . Large, contiguous blocks of space are especially rare. Although the building has a Park Avenue address, it is south of Grand Central Terminal and therefore doesn't qualify as part of the prized submarket. Vornado’s 350 Park Ave ., being constructed for hedge fund Citadel with a $3.3B loan , does. Average weighted rents at 90 Park Ave. are $87 per SF, according to Vornado's Q3 earnings supplemental report , above the $76.83-per-SF asking rent for all offices. The tower’s other major tenant is PwC , which leases 240K SF . MassMutual and Glencore also fill roughly 45K SF each. The building’s base is 96% occupied, with Citibank and Starbucks as its largest retail tenants. Vornado has greatly benefited from New York City’s market recovery, which leads the country. It signed tenants to 1.1M SF of leases through the first nine months of the year at an average initial rent of $113.09 per SF. Last year, Chairman and CEO Steven Roth expressed interest in selling assets elsewhere to focus on the well-performing properties in the city. items.title: New-home sales post unexpected surge in October
items.description: New-home sales post unexpected surge in October by John Yellig November 25, 2026 The pace of new single-family home sales blew past analyst expectations in October, posting an annual rate of 701,000, the U.S. Census Bureau and Department of Housing and Urban Development said. The consensus estimate was for the pace to decline from 676,000 in September to 670,000 last month. “Even with mortgage rates at their highest since 2023, buyers turned out for homes they could afford,” First American Deputy Chief Economist Odeta Kushi said. "Builders have kept sales moving by offering lower-priced homes and helping buyers with financing. Heading into winter, how much more of the monthly payment can builders afford to buy down?” October’s results represented a 14.2% increase over September’s downwardly revised estimate of 614,000 sales and a 7.5% gain from the October 2025 rate of 652,000 sales. The median sales price of new homes in October was $391,300, representing declines of 0.3% month over month and 3.2% year over year. The seasonally adjusted estimate of new houses for sale at the end of October was 470,000, down 1.5% from September and 4.1% from October 2025. That represented a supply of 8.0 months at the current sales rate. “The contrast with the struggling resale market comes down to what it costs a seller to wait,” Kushi said. “A homeowner with a low mortgage rate can join the sellers’ strike and stay put, especially if moving means accepting a lower price on the current home and a higher mortgage rate on the next one. Builders face a different calculation. items.title: Houston Gas Station Boom Faces Potential Roadblock As City Weighs Location Restrictions
items.description: With a lack of zoning, plentiful land, no shortage of cars and tax breaks that boost returns for investors, Houston has been the state’s top market for gas station development. Unsplash/Aron Yigin Some think developers have become too eager. The demolition of a historic mansion for a potential convenience store project and calls for a moratorium have brought the wave of investment into hyperfocus and could stymie further growth. The Houston City Council plans to consider an ordinance placing restrictions on gas station projects, a rare move for a city famous for its lack of a traditional citywide zoning ordinance. The proposal could have prohibited 50 of the 188 Houston projects applied for over the past four years. Dhanani Private Equity Group has developed more than 60 24 Seven convenience stores around the Houston area but began diversifying its portfolio about six years ago due to market saturation, the rise of electric vehicles and increased construction costs , President Nikhil Dhanani said . He supports the creation of restrictions that would force new gas stations to spread out more throughout Houston. “It’s better for everybody,” Dhanani said. “It's more profitable. I've seen people lose their shirts building just right next to each other, just because they can do it.” Harris County had 231 facilities apply for gasoline or diesel storage tank permits since the start of 2023, more than four times as many as any other county in the state, according to Texas Commission on Environmental Quality data analyzed by Bisnow . Houston’s proposed ordinance, scheduled for consideration in January, would largely forbid new gas station projects on roads that are 80 feet or narrower, if they are surrounded primarily by residential buildings. Of the 188 fuel station applications within city limits over the past four years, 27% were on roads 80 feet wide or less, and 52% had homes within 100 feet, according to data from the mayor’s office. A proposed project in Riverside Terrace, which residents opposed , would not qualify under the ordinance, though applicants would be allowed to apply for a variance. Developers want to build gas stations and convenience stores because they can often stabilize and sell a property within a year, a much shorter timeline than other asset classes like multifamily and hospitality, said Sai Thakor , a vice president at CBRE . Investors are chasing assets in the gas station and convenience store sector, resulting in some of retail’s tightest cap rates. The demand is propped up by 100% bonus depreciation and is unimpaired by elevated and volatile gas prices. items.title: MBA: Mortgage applications surge on purchase activity
items.description: MBA: Mortgage applications surge on purchase activity by John Yellig November 25, 2026 A jump in purchase applications sent total mortgage applications higher in the week ended Nov. 20, the Mortgage Bankers Association reported, citing its Market Composite Index . Purchase applications climbed 10% week over week, while refinance applications rose just 1%. Altogether, the index rose 6.1%. The increases came despite the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hitting 7.38%, its highest level in five weeks, MBA Deputy Chief Economist Joel Kan said. “Purchase applications reached their strongest weekly pace since September but remained well behind last year’s pace,” Kan said. "A larger share of borrowers relied on ARM loans for lower monthly payments, which accounted for 11.5% of applications, the highest share in more than a year." At 6.39%, the ARM mortgage rate was nearly a full percentage lower than the 30-year fixed rate last week, Kan noted.
