items.description: Fairstead Closes $17M Affordable Housing Transaction in Oklahoma Fairstead announced its $16.5 million acquisition of London Square Village Apartments, a 200-unit project-based Section 8 community in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, and plans for a comprehensive rehabilitation of the property. The transaction marks Fairstead’s first acquisition in Oklahoma. London Square Village Apartments consists of 200 units across 18 two-story residential buildings and a community center. The community includes 24 one-bedroom, 96 two-bedroom and 80 three-bedroom homes, with all units reserved for households earning at or below 60% of the area median income. “Expanding into Oklahoma represents an important step in Fairstead’s mission to preserve sustainable, reliable affordable housing for communities across the country,” said Jeff Goldberg, Founder and CEO of Fairstead. items.title: No, the Mavericks Probably Aren't Moving to City Hall (Still)
items.description: Live Poll The City Council will have a special called meeting on December 1 to discuss two things, and those two things have caused my phone to blow up with people asking if one of those things is the thing they’re worried about the most. I can tell you I’m 99 percent certain it is not the thing you are worried about the most, if the thing you are worried about the most is whether the city will decide to yoink its I.M. Pei-designed Brutalist City Hall off 1500 Marilla to build an entertainment district. The agenda lists two items, and it’s not clear that both are related. First, a closed session to “discuss or deliberate commercial or financial information the city has received from a business prospect (Project X) that the city seeks to have locate, stay, or expand in or near” Dallas. The city is also “conducting economic development negotiations” with this prospect, and could offer “financial or other incentives” in connection with the project. Second on the agenda is a potential vote to authorize an economic development agreement between the city and Dallas Basketball Limited or an affiliate “regarding development of a sports and entertainment district anchored by a new multipurpose arena.” The term sheet would be discussed in closed session. All finalists will be featured in the April 2027 issue of D CEO , online at D CEO Real Estate , and honored at an exclusive awards event. Learn More Who is Dallas Basketball Limited? That’s the Dallas Mavericks. Nine of the 10 queries I received yesterday afternoon and evening about this meeting were concerns that the Council was going to vote on something that would bring the Mavericks to the City Hall site. I do not think this is the case. A source familiar with the proposed Valley View purchase who spoke on background tells me the deal is progressing, and even "accelerating.” This jibes with what we’ve previously reported: The team hired Legends Global in July as its owner’s representative to act as “an independent third-party representing the Mavericks from pre-design through closeout, protecting the team’s interests in budgeting, construction schedules, quality, and risk control, while also serving as a liaison to contractors and architects.” In September , the organization said it was ready to begin working with the city to amend a planned development already in existence and create a subdistrict that would allow a sports and entertainment district. The impending retirement of CEO Rick Welts , who was brought on board primarily to help the team secure a new site for an arena, could be a sign that the Valley View site is pretty secure. The Mavs front office continues to tell us that the site is Valley View. So what could be happening? Our first clue is the type of agreement the agenda mentions. A Chapter 380 Economic Development Agreement allows a Texas city to offer financial incentives to encourage private development through grants, loans, city services, or performance-based incentives. The draft resolution the Council will vote on says that the Mavericks and the city “have developed the general terms and conditions for a proposed public-private partnership” for the development of a new arena to be built in an entertainment district. It doesn’t specify what kind of financial incentives, the source of the funding, or whether the Mall Area Redevelopment TIF is involved. (The Valley View site is in the Dallas International District just north of LBJ, within a barbell TIF, which links the Valley View and Red Bird areas so growth in property tax revenue in one can help fund improvements in the other.) It also doesn’t say where the arena would be built. The resolution would also authorize Tolbert to negotiate and execute an arena lease, a non-relocation agreement, documents establishing a local government corporation, and a community benefits agreement. All would be based on a nonbinding term sheet discussed behind closed doors. In other words, the Council isn't merely being asked to authorize further conversations with the Mavericks, but to give Tolbert the runway to execute any resulting agreements. In October, Welts indicated that there would likely be some public money involved in the construction of the arena, couching it as an “ongoing discussion we’re having with the city right now.” . “And I think public investment at some level is very justified because I do think what professional sports teams bring to any city enhances the quality of life for a lot of people,” he added. “So it’s up to any city to make their own decision about what they feel a level of investment that can be justified. But I think it’s money well spent.” It’s also worth noting that Tolbert has not yet presented the Council with a report outlining the costs and options for moving out of City Hall and developing it. ( It was due in August .) The Save Dallas City Hall Coalition just turned in nearly 35,000 signatures to put a charter amendment codifying that 1500 Marilla is Dallas’ seat of city government on a ballot in May, pending signature verification. The Council will meet at 1 p.m. on December 1. You can sign up to speak here , and can watch the proceedings here . Keep up with all the new Mavericks arena and City Hall discussions here . items.title: The Stars Are Holding Steady. Is That a Good Thing?
items.description: Live Poll This time a year ago, the Stars had a points percentage of .682 through their first 22 games. That was good for a 13-4-2 record. Through their first 22 games this season, the Stars have a points percentage of .682 with a 14-6-2 record. Déjà vu? Pretty much, for good reasons and bad. Let’s start with the good, of which there is plenty. The Stars under Glen Gulutzan continue to check all the right boxes. Teams in playoff position by Thanksgiving have a 77 percent chance to qualify for the postseason. The Stars will qualify, and there’s a very good chance they qualify as one of the best teams in one of the best divisions because Dallas profiles like a proper contender . In both years under Gulutzan, the Stars have been in the top 10 in percentage of goals and percentage of expected goals. Special teams have been broadly reliable. Mikko Rantanen and Jason Robertson are on blistering point paces. Rantanen is on track for 102 points through 84, while Robertson doesn’t lag far behind, with 95. The dynamic duo tallied nine points in that two-game series versus Vegas, illustrating the X-factor the Stars will have as long as they employ two game-changing wingers. In the middle, Roope Hintz is on pace to crack 80 points, which would be a career high. Beyond the forwards, the blue line is quietly putting together a strong season. Miro Heiskanen and Thomas Harley are on pace to clear 50 points. Heiskanen’s two-way presence will never be in doubt, but Harley keeping pace with Heiskanen despite playing limited power-play minutes is encouraging after a rough 2025-26 campaign. And after following up an outstanding October with some early November scares, Jake Oettinger looks primed to erase last year’s performance from memory. He is currently third in goals saved above expected per MoneyPuck , behind only Jesper Wallstedt and Jacob Fowler. I’ve been keeping track of what I like to call “the power nine.” It’s nothing fancy, just a collection of various categories you will recognize as traditional keys to victory, expressed as percentages. They come from Louis Boulet’s postgame reports . The best part? They are statistically significant as factors that determine wins . While Dallas doesn’t have Thanos’ gauntlet around its fist, a few key stones are already in place. The most encouraging part of this data is that the Stars are not just good at most things; they’re great in a few, too. Dallas is dominating the special teams battle, the net-front factor (which is calculated by looking at the combination of rebounds a team generates along with their expected rebounds), and faceoffs. Again, each of these are statistically significant. I suppose this is the part where I turn into Ebeneezer Scrooge. If everything feels so familiar, then the real question is: are the concerns familiar, too? Unfortunately for Dallas, yes. Revisiting the Vegas games is a worthwhile exercise because it encapsulates a lot of the worries from last season. At 5v5, Dallas was outshot 42-30 and outscored 5-4. The gamestates the Stars leveraged to eke out a win—overtime and 3v3—won’t be available in the playoffs. Last season, the Stars were 30th in shot attempts-for per hour. This season, they’re 25th. Last season, they were 21st in expected goals-for at 5v5. This season, they’re 23rd. That won’t cut it, and Gulutzan acknowledged as much in his Friday postgame presser . “We’ve got a better game we need to put on the table moving forward,” he told Mike Heika. Dallas didn’t show it on Sunday versus Pittsburgh, getting outshot by the worst team in the East. Even the high-danger chance differential, an area Dallas tends to keep closer, was skewed in the Penguins' favor. Gulutzan, to his credit, has talked openly about what the Stars need—namely, a fix for the 5v5 offense. The team has transitioned to a different forecheck, and there are tactical differences, such as their breakouts , that appear to be paying some dividends. But so far, a lot of the same issues that worried me in April , January , and even May of 2025 remain. Things could change. A healthy Matt Duchene should move the needle, and Jim Nill could pull another rabbit out of his hat at the trade deadline despite Dallas' being cap-strapped. But it’s not like there have been zero surprises to compensate. Arttu Hyry has been an absolute boon as the kind of depth player the Stars haven’t had in years, the rare bottom-six forward who can play up the lineup . Clarkson University alumnus Trey Taylor continues to look like an everyday NHLer in his brief stint. Even if another prospect makes the jump, or if the Stars make an impact deadline addition, what does that truly change? The core needs to shift into a core that can dictate the rules of engagement, and that doesn’t come easy. Without that, Dallas will stay on the same collision course as last season, where the division (not to mention playoff seeding) is unforgiving. Assuming the current point paces hold, Minnesota will finish first, followed by Dallas and then Colorado. That’s a two-round gauntlet just to have the privilege of a crack at a team like Edmonton. If the Stars finally get out of the West, an Eastern Conference heavy hitter like Carolina awaits them in the Stanley Cup Final. Unsurprisingly, many have called this season a transition year. Once the Stars have $34 million in cap room to play with this offseason, then they become a Cup favorite. But is there such a thing as a transition year when Rantanen and Robertson are having the years they’re having? Heiskanen and Harley? Oettinger is on pace for 33 goals saved above expected. Not only would that be his best year to date, but it would be a top-20 performance in the modern era. For now, the team is relatively healthy. Why not capitalize? Déjà vu is great when it’s all positive. But the Stars need some novelty in order to avoid another first-round playoff heartache. items.title: Rate introduces new home equity loan, EquitySimple
items.description: Rate introduces new home equity loan, EquitySimple by John Yellig November 25, 2026 Rate recently launched EquitySimple, a new fixed-rate, flat-fee home equity loan that can close in as little as 14 days. Homeowners can use EquitySimple to consolidate higher-interest debt, lower monthly payments, fund home improvements or cover major expenses. Whereas the average credit card interest rate is currently above 21%, according to the Federal Reserve, most of Rate’s fixed-rate home equity loans have carried interest rates under 8% this year, Rate said. The terms of the loans are designed to be simple, according to Rate : One rate, one payment and one fee. Homeowners with low mortgage rates on their homes can keep them as is, as the EquitySimple loan is a separate loan. “Too many homeowners are paying credit card interest rates above 20% while sitting on significant equity they’ve worked hard to build,” Rate Founder and CEO Victor Ciardelli said. “We’re committed to helping our members build the good life around home, health and wealth, but financial stress can get in the way. That’s why we built EquitySimple: to give homeowners real relief and real options, with one fixed rate, one predictable payment and real advice when they want it, so they can pay down what’s weighing on them, close that chapter and start looking forward.” EquitySimple is available in 49 states plus Washington, D.C. It is not available in Texas. items.title: Snowbird season in South Florida: How part-time residents manage two homes
items.description: Snowbird season in South Florida: How part-time residents manage two homes by South Florida Agent November 24, 2026 Spending part of the year in South Florida and the rest somewhere farther north offers an appealing lifestyle. Snowbirds enjoy warmer winters, escape colder temperatures and maintain connections to two different communities. However, managing two properties comes with responsibilities that can become complicated without a consistent plan. From transporting personal belongings to protecting an unoccupied home during hurricane season, seasonal residents need to think beyond simply locking the door before leaving. A few practical habits can make maintaining two homes much easier. 1. Keep essentials in both homes One of the biggest mistakes first-time snowbirds make is transporting too many belongings between properties. Packing and unpacking twice a year creates unnecessary work, especially when many everyday items are inexpensive to replace. Reserve transportation space for items that are valuable, personal or difficult to replace. Important documents, medication, jewellery, laptops and sentimental possessions may be worth carrying between locations. A useful rule is to compare the cost of buying a second item with the inconvenience of transporting it twice a year. If purchasing another one is cheaper and easier, keep one at each property. 2. Prepare your florida property before leaving South Florida's summer climate creates several challenges for homes left unoccupied for extended periods. Heat, humidity and heavy rainfall can contribute to mold, water damage and other maintenance problems. Humidity control should be a priority. Rather than switching off the air conditioning completely, consider maintaining a suitable temperature or using a dedicated dehumidifier. Check the manufacturer's recommendations and arrange for regular monitoring to ensure the system continues working. Other useful preparations include: Emptying and cleaning the refrigerator. Removing perishable food and rubbish. Covering upholstered furniture. Moving important belongings away from windows and floors. Arranging hurricane shutters or other storm protection. Checking smoke detectors and security systems. These steps reduce the likelihood of returning to unexpected maintenance problems. 3. Use storage to keep both properties organized Maintaining two homes can gradually lead to clutter. Furniture, seasonal decorations, unused appliances and boxes often accumulate in the Florida property because there is nowhere else to put them. A separate storage arrangement can help prevent this. Climate-controlled storage is particularly useful for belongings that may be damaged by South Florida's heat and humidity, including wooden furniture, leather items, electronics, photographs and important documents. Working with local providers that offer both relocation and storage services, such as Pro Movers Miami , can simplify the process. Having one company coordinate transportation and storage may also reduce the number of arrangements required each season. 4. Schedule moves outside peak snowbird periods Most seasonal residents follow similar travel patterns. Many head south between October and early December, then return north during March and April. For larger relocations, contact service providers several weeks ahead and confirm appointments before making travel arrangements. 5. Keep insurance and administrative details updated Two residences also mean managing two sets of property-related responsibilities. Mail forwarding, utility accounts, vehicle insurance, registrations and delivery addresses should all be reviewed before each seasonal departure. Also, make sure important deliveries are redirected, subscriptions are updated and someone can receive urgent correspondence while you are away. 6. Arrange regular property checks Even a properly prepared home needs occasional attention. A trusted neighbour, property manager or professional service should be able to inspect the property while you are away. Regular checks can identify plumbing leaks, storm damage, electrical issues, pest activity or air-conditioning failures before they become expensive problems. Make seasonal living easier Managing two homes becomes much simpler when responsibilities are organized before each departure. Keeping duplicate essentials, preparing the Florida property, arranging suitable storage and maintaining regular inspections can prevent many common problems. With a reliable seasonal routine and a little advance planning, snowbirds can spend less time worrying about property management and more time enjoying everything South Florida has to offer. items.description: The Cuans joins Coldwell Banker in Coral Gables by John Yellig November 24, 2026 The Cuans, a family-led real estate team in Miami, has joined Coldwell Banker Realty's Coral Gables office. The team serves homeowners, investors, builders and developers across Coral Gables, Coconut Grove, South Miami, Pinecrest and adjacent emerging areas. It specializes in luxury homes , investment properties, land and new development. Since 2021, the team has closed nearly $200 million in sales, including more than $45 million this year. items.title: What's driving seller confidence in 2026
items.description: What's driving seller confidence in 2026 by Elizabeth Kanzeg Rowland November 23, 2026 Sellers put in the research to understand pricing and mortgage rates, leading to higher levels of confidence in the selling process. Uncertain rate outlooks and affordability concerns failed to dampen seller confidence in 2026, according to a new Ipsos study commissioned by Century 21 Real Estate. The group's Home Seller Confidence Report revealed high levels of confidence as sellers balance optimal pricing with the emotional drivers behind a move. Over 1,000 Americans over the age of 21 who were current, prospective or recent home sellers were interviewed for the study. So what's driving the trend? Sellers who prioritize strategy, researchers noted. Secure sellers Sellers have few qualms about selling in today's market conditions. Among homeowners planning to sell within 12 months, 75% believe now is the right time to move. So do 82% of those whose homes were already listed. Seller confidence may be age-dependent, researchers found. A substantial 83% of sellers aged 21 to 34 expressed confidence that now is the right time to sell. Meanwhile, sellers aged 35 to 54 and sellers aged 55-plus reported confidence at rates of 78% and 58%, respectively. What's moving movers? Mortgage rates influenced sellers' actions, but personal incentives drove decisions too. Of sellers interviewed, 86% said their mortgage rate was slightly, moderately, very or extremely influential on the timing of their move. Giving up an auspicious mortgage rate created a pain point for many sellers, with 63% of sellers with a mortgage rate below 5% stating that giving up their rate was emotionally difficult and 54% of all sellers agreeing that giving up their rate was harder than leaving their home. Around 19% of sellers listed mortgage rates as their top reason for moving. But personal reasons were given more often, like change of scenery (27%), finding their next home (25%), a personal life event (22%) and feeling emotionally ready (21%). “Mortgage rates are a big part of the housing conversation, but people don't make decisions about their homes based on rates alone,” said Mike Miedler, president and CEO of Century 21 Real Estate. “New jobs, growing families and other life changes still motivate people to move. Sellers aren't waiting for perfect conditions, but they are approaching that decision with more thought and preparation. They want to understand what their home is worth and how quickly it could sell so they can move forward with confidence.” The pricing problem Many sellers expressed concern over getting the best possible price for their home. This priority became especially pronounced with older sellers. Almost half (47%) of sellers 55-plus listed getting the highest possible sales price as the most important outcome when selling their home. This percentage dropped to 32% for sellers aged 35 to 54 and just 16% for sellers aged 21 to 34. Uncertainty about proper pricing led 58% of all sellers to worry about pricing too high and 27% to worry about pricing too low. Notably, 66% of sellers who sold in the last 24 months seriously reconsidered or changed their asking price before listing — some over four times. Of this cohort, however, 35% never ended up changing the price at all throughout the selling process. Where sellers turn In response to uncertainties like pricing, sellers seek information and guidance. Some look to real estate professionals. The study found that agents have influence over seller pricing decisions. Of sellers who listed with an agent, 59% followed their agent’s pricing recommendation. Other sellers turned to AI, with 54% of sellers saying that AI gave them significantly or somewhat more confidence while selling their home. Around 67% of recent and prospective sellers used AI for tasks like estimating home values, studying local market conditions and researching where to move next. However, many sellers recognized AI's limitations, especially when it came to providing pricing accuracy instead of placating with optimistic estimates. For sellers who compared an agent's recommendation with an AI pricing estimate, 45% reported that their agent was closer to their final sale price. Overall, 46% of those who compared AI and their agent’s pricing advice trusted the agent more, while just 15% trusted AI more. The big picture Strategy and security drive seller choices. Sellers put in the research to understand pricing and mortgage rates, leading to higher levels of confidence in the selling process. “Today's sellers are approaching one of life's biggest financial decisions with more research and intention than ever before,” said Miedler. “They're exploring pricing strategies, evaluating buyer demand and looking for trusted guidance before bringing their homes to market. items.title: Judge Upholds Mamdani’s NYC Rent Freeze, Tosses Landlords’ Lawsuit
items.description: A Manhattan judge has upheld New York City 's rent freeze for roughly 1 million rent-stabilized apartments , dismissing a lawsuit brought by landlords who argued that the decision was politically predetermined. In a 20-page ruling issued on Wednesday, New York Supreme Court Justice Brendan T. Lantry found that the city's Rent Guidelines Board had acted within its authority when it voted this summer to freeze rents on both one- and two-year leases. The landlords, led by Kenilworth Holdings LLC, argued that Mayor Zohran Mamdani had effectively dictated the outcome after campaigning on a promise to freeze rents and appointing board members who supported the policy. Judge criticizes Mamdani but upholds freeze Despite the favorable ruling, Lantry wasn't entirely sympathetic to the mayor. In his final decision, he called Mamdani's campaign promise "reckless and irresponsible." Even so, he concluded that the board had independently considered the evidence before reaching its decision. Loading... Mayor Zohran Mamdani's rent freeze is a central piece of his housing affordability agenda, alongside his Block by Block plan to build 200,000 affordable homes and preserve another 200,000 over the next decade. NYC Mayor's Office The freeze passed in June after a landmark 7-1 vote , with only Arpit Gupta , an economist who was appointed to the board in 2022 by Mayor Eric Adams , voting no. But it was owner-representative Maksim Wynn 's statement that stoked controversy at the meeting, after he raised concerns about the financial health of the city's buildings. Wynn's full statement was drowned out by boos from the crowd before he ultimately voted in favor of the freeze. Those pressures were central to the landlords' suit, which argued that a "rent freeze is impossible to reconcile" with such rising costs, pointing to mounting expenses for insurance, maintenance, utilities, and property taxes. Operating and maintenance expenses consumed roughly 71 cents of every dollar of revenue in 2024, according to the board's 2026 Income and Expense Study. And as Realtor.com® previously reported, those figures exclude mortgage payments and major capital expenses, which landlords argue can leave otherwise profitable-looking buildings struggling financially. “Freezing rent sounds like a sure-fire way to solve housing affordability, but what I'm worried about is the unintended consequences on the rent-stabilized stock and market-rate prices,” Jake Krimmel , s enior economist at Realtor.com , said in June. Lantry acknowledged that potential fallout, writing that the freeze could have "detrimental impacts on the New York City residential real estate industry." But he emphasized that weighing the wisdom of the policy was not the court's role, writing that the freeze "has a rational basis and must therefore be upheld as valid." The ruling leaves the freeze intact; however, the landlords could seek to appeal. Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

items.title: Mortgage Rates Dip, Offering Moderate Relief to Buyers Ahead of Thanksgiving as Fed Rate Hike Looms
items.description: Mortgage rates have pulled back this week as AI investment trade creates volatility in financial markets and Treasury yields fall back below 5%. The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans dropped to 7.21% for the week ending Nov. 25, down 7 basis points from 7.28% recorded the week before, according to Freddie Mac . For perspective, rates averaged 6.26% one year ago. “Mortgage rates moved back down this week, offering modest relief for prospective homebuyers heading into the Thanksgiving holiday,” says Sam Khater , Freddie Mac's chief economist. It is all but guaranteed that the Federal Reserve will raise its benchmark rate to curb inflation at the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting on Dec. 8. The looming hike, combined with the persistence of the war in Iran, pushed the 10-year Treasury yield back toward 4.816% this week, putting mortgage rates on an upward trajectory once again. The AI investment trade has created volatility in financial markets as investors try to value companies, including the Anthropic IPO, which gave the company a valuation greater than the value of every home currently listed for sale . AI-generated wealth is already shaping consumer housing behavior , with San Francisco Bay Area buyers and those in other tech hubs leaning toward higher down payments. Markets are currently pricing a 97.6% chance of a 25-basis-point increase next month, according to the CME FedWatch tool. Meanwhile, pending home sales fell to a record low in October , and existing-home sales hit their lowest level since 2010 , as the surge in mortgage rates through mid-October took its toll on buyers and sellers. What this means for buyers For buyers who remain active in the market, current conditions offer some meaningful advantages, including less competition from other shoppers, inventory climbing 8.6% year over year, and sellers increasingly willing to negotiate on price. This week, the median listing price fell 2.4% from a year ago to $400,000, according to the latest Realtor.com weekly housing market update . "The challenge is that until inflation cools enough to put mortgage rates on a durable downward path, affordability will remain the dominant constraint on the market," says Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith . A credit score will determine whether you qualify for a mortgage and the interest rate you'll receive. The higher the credit score, the lower the interest rate you'll qualify for. The credit score you need will vary depending on the type of loan. A score of 620 is a "fair" rating. However, people applying for a Federal Housing Administration loan might be able to get approved with a credit score of 500, which is considered a low score. Homebuyers with credit scores of 740 or higher are typically considered to be in very good standing and can usually qualify for better rates, which can reduce monthly payments. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

items.title: How real estate agents handle proof of funds and disclosures
items.description: On a recent coaching call this week, an agent asked a question that looks tactical and is actually about professional discipline. She works mostly in commercial, she has a physician buying a home and several of her clients have investors behind them, which makes gathering proof of funds a real ordeal. When do I ask for it? Does it need to be current? And how do I protect something that private? Those questions sit squarely on the line between being a salesperson and being a fiduciary, and that line is where our industry keeps getting tested. Let me give the coaching first, because the sequence is where most agents go wrong. It's all about the sequence Proof of funds gets requested too early and in the wrong tone. Imagine a buyer who just called on an ad. If the first thing you do is hand them a list of documents, you have converted a warm first contact into homework, and you have done it before you have given them a single reason to trust you. I do not open any client relationship by burdening the person with tasks. The order has to serve the relationship, not the file. Here is the sequence I teach. Get them into the office first. On that opening call you can ask one soft question, do you happen to have a proof of funds ready, and if the answer is no, you keep it light. We will need it at some point, bring it when we meet if you can, but do not worry about it now. You have raised the flag without turning it into a barrier. When they arrive, run a genuine buyer appointment and get the buyer to hire you, the same way you would work to get hired by a seller. Only then do you assign the homework, and now the identical list that would have felt like a wall on the phone lands as a plan. Here is what we need from you, and in the meantime let's define exactly what you are looking for, let me show you what is available, and we can even see a couple so you get a feel for the market. The serious looking begins once I have the documents. The buyer never feels interrogated. They feel represented. Powerfact: You earn the right to ask for documents by first earning the relationship. This is what matters Now to the part that matters for leaders, because it is about how we protect our businesses and our clients at the same time. She asked whether to send buyers to their own bank or recommend someone she knows. I prefer to recommend my own lender, and I say that carefully, because we are operating in a litigation environment, and the professional move is to assume you could be sued and to run your business so that you are covered. Practically, that means disclosing any financial relationship in writing, every time. On our coaching platform I built a document I call the Transparency Conversation, a simple editable form that states who you are connected to, how you get paid, and whether anyone shares in a fee. If the lender is tied to your company and a financial arrangement exists, that gets disclosed plainly. If you are recommending someone purely because you know and trust the loan officer, you say exactly that and nothing more. Here is how I used to present the recommendation itself, and the logic has aged well. You can use any lender you want, that is your call. The reason I like my person is this. I could refer a lot of lenders, and I choose this one, because if he ever lets you down, he does not just lose your loan, he loses every piece of business I will ever send him. So he will do whatever it takes, within the rules, to get you to the closing table. That framing respects the buyer's freedom and explains why your recommendation carries weight. It is service, stated out loud. Her question was about confidentiality. She had a buyer with roughly $2 million in proof of funds, and people are private about money at that level. Does it become confidential? Do we keep the figure quiet even though we hold the documentation? This is where the fiduciary line gets drawn. The moment a buyer hires you, they stop being a customer and become a client, and that shift carries a duty. Anything they share with you stays with you unless they authorize otherwise. So think like an attorney. When the information is this sensitive, you protect it with a document. Have the client sign an authorization that permits you to share their financial information only with the parties who truly need it to assemble the transaction. You can adapt the Transparency Conversation form for exactly this. Now you can do your job, the client's privacy is respected, and you have a record that protects both of you. There was one more exchange worth passing on Another agent said she never provides proof of funds until after an offer is accepted. That is a sound default in many cases, but it depends on the seller. On luxury homes, estates, and commercial property, the listing side will often require proof of funds before they open the door, and that is legitimate. Sellers of a multimillion dollar property do not want a stream of non-buyers touring for decorating ideas or dream-board photos. When you represent that buyer, prepare them for the requirement so a reasonable request does not feel like an insult. For brokers and team leaders, here is the translation. Our industry has spent two years being told that our compensation and our value must be disclosed, documented, and justified. Good. The agents who will thrive under that scrutiny are the ones who already behave like fiduciaries by habit, not the ones who treat disclosure as a form to dodge. Teach your people the sequence, relationship first, documents second. Standardize the written disclosures so no agent is improvising a legal boundary on the fly. And model the confidentiality, because a buyer who sees you guard their two million dollar statement like it is your own will refer you for the rest of their life. The whole thing fits on one page. items.title: BOXABL financial filing shows cash burn and scaling risk
items.description: [Editor's note: HousingWire TBD author Dan Oppenheim contributed financial analysis and insight for this report.] Factory-built housing’s promise of a not-so-distant brighter future has always been compelling. Forever, it seems, it has carried an “always within five years” sense of inevitability, stuck in limbo. Build homes faster, with less waste, fewer labor constraints, greater consistency, in conditioned indoor offsite space, and at costs low enough to bend asking-price curves toward households priced out of homeownership. The arrival of housing’s future, however, seems caught in the unforgiving calculus of time and space's infinite divisibility. Progress happens and promises soar, but the ultimate goal of powering United States home development and construction with modern manufacturing going concerns keeps falling short, trapped in an echo chamber of not-exactly-here and not-quite-yet. The rub has always been turning the promise of housing’s future into a business that can reliably produce homes, deliver them to customers, cover its costs, and generate enough cash to keep doing it. Many homebuilding business leaders who’ve tried a lot of things and kept doing what works are apt to think of all that as homebuilding’s never-ending siren’s song, one that, should it emerge, should be dispelled as a wishful-thinking distraction. BOXABL , the Las Vegas-based modular housing manufacturer that completed its Nasdaq listing in July, now faces that test amid mounting difficulties, including self-inflicted ones. Its November 16, 2026, quarterly filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission provides data to address questions that experienced homebuilding executives have long raised about factory-based housing ventures and that they have expressed about BOXABLE. Can a manufacturer achieve sufficient production volume to absorb fixed costs? Can it coordinate factory output with site readiness, permitting, installation, and customer financing? And can it sustain those operations when capital is expensive, construction inputs remain inflation-pressured, and affordability-constrained homebuyers are wavering for any of half a dozen good reasons? BOXABL's filing shows progress in generating orders. It also shows that the company's operating model still falls far short of demonstrating the economic soundness, scalability, and durability required to sustain a residential construction business. The company's options have not disappeared, but they have narrowed, and time is quickly passing. Management has less room and less time to demonstrate the business’s financial sustainability. The financial reality behind the promise BOXABL's Form 10-Q, filed on November 16 for the quarter ended September 30, reports $14 million in unrestricted cash, down from $29 million at year-end 2025. During the most recent quarter, the company used $6 million in cash for operations, down from $8.4 million in the third quarter of 2025. This translates to a cash burn rate of about $2 million per month, so the $14 million of unrestricted cash on hand as of the end of Q3 represents seven months of operations. That metric doesn’t precisely forecast when BOXABL might run out of cash. Instead, it shows the relationship between available resources and BOXABL’s most recent cash-burn rate. In Note 4 of the filing, the company states: "Substantial doubt about the Company's ability to continue as a going concern exists." Is the disclosure a prediction of failure? Technically and officially, no. Management identifies continued cost controls, accelerated Casita deliveries and sales, and additional equity financing as measures intended to address the uncertainty. There’s no ambiguity that those measures must deliver results even as the company continues to consume cash. To BOXABL’s credit, the company would significantly improve its cash flow if it converts more of its backlog into revenue. For a modular housing company to succeed, it must 1) demonstrate customer acceptance of its product and pricing through customer orders, 2) translate that acceptance into sufficient volume to build homes efficiently and absorb overhead, and 3) execute effectively in converting the backlog into finished sales. BOXABL’s Q3 results show progress on the first item (customer orders), but it still has a lot of ground to cover on items 2 (efficient construction and overhead absorption) and 3 (converting the backlog into revenue). Orders grow; deliveries not so much BOXABL reported 209 net orders for Casitas in Q3, bringing its total for the first nine months to 362 net orders. As of September 30, the company had 679 Casitas in backlog, representing approximately $45 million in potential revenue. Those figures indicate customer interest but raise what are arguably the most important questions for BOXABL – how legitimate the orders are, how much of the backlog will convert to revenue, and when that conversion will occur. The point is that while most homebuilders count a signed contract as an order only after the customer has satisfied mortgage qualification, BOXABL notes that 85 Casitas in the backlog (and recorded as an order during a recent quarter) are pending feasibility studies to assess whether the customer’s site can support installation. In addition, another 311 units in the backlog were associated with orders that were one to two years old, raising questions about whether they will convert to revenue. Together, these 396 units, the 85 units that still require feasibility assessment, and the 311 older orders represent 58% of the company’s reported backlog of 679 units. Regarding converting backlog into revenue, at the end of Q2, BOXABL had 479 units in backlog and 189 finished units in inventory. items.title: Epique’s ‘Power Agent’ trademark fight could put its branding at risk
items.description: Darryl Davis Seminars Inc.’s multi-million dollar federal trademark infringement lawsuit against Epique Realty , which accuses the virtual brokerage of unlawfully using the POWER AGENT® brand in its nationwide operations, is headed to court next week. During the first week of December, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York will hold a hearing on a motion for a preliminary injunction filed by Darryl Davis and his firm that would bar Epique Realty , a RealTrends Verified brokerage, from using the POWER AGENT trademark. Originally filed in late June , the lawsuit alleges that Houston-based Epique Realty adopted the POWER AGENT name and “built an entire brand architecture around it” despite being put on notice and asked to stop, according to the announcement. In addition to Epique Realty, the lawsuit also lists Joshua Miller , Janice Delcid , Christopher Miller, XYZ Corps 1-10 and John and Jane Does 1-10 as defendants. Darryl Davis Seminars says it has used the POWER AGENT mark continuously since 1993 through The POWER Program, which it describes as the real estate industry’s oldest and longest-running agent training and coaching platform. "POWER AGENT® has been our name since 1993, and both it and THE POWER PROGRAM® are registered trademarks," Davis told HousingWire. "The law expects a trademark owner to protect its marks. We have for decades, and we will keep doing so. Because the matter is pending, I will let our court filings speak to the rest." Counterclaims filed In October, Epique filed a counterclaim asking for a ruling from the court that Davis’s trademark registrations of Power Agent programs do not give his firm exclusive rights to the word “power” and that this does not give Davis or his company the rights to a family of “Power” trademarks. Epique is also asking the court to force Davis and his firm to prove likely confusing for each expression of “Power” Epique was accused of. Epique is also seeking rulings from the court that its current uses of PowerFlex and PowerCon, do not infringe on Davis’s trademarks and that it is not liable “merely because an independently controlled agent or third party used POWER-formative wording.” Epique emphasized in the filing that its agents are independent contractors and that the company does not hold passwords for agents’ personal social media accounts in order to edit or delete content, nor does it review agents’ social media posts or websites before they are published. This contradicts Davis’s complaint, which alleges that the brokerage’s independent contractor agreement requires agents to submit marketing or advertising posts for approval prior to publication. Additionally, the company said that under state law in Texas, where Epique is headquartered, the firm is only responsible for ensuring that advertising content produced by agents complies with state rules. In a filing earlier this month, Davis largely denied Epique’s counterclaims, namely that he is trying to trademark the word “Power” by itself and he and his firm rejected Epique’s request that the court declares that Darryl Davis Seminars does not own the word "power" exclusively and that it does not have an across-the-board monopoly over trademarks containing the word. Throughout the filing, Davis maintained that Epique infringed on his firm’s trademarks and he asked the court to reject Epique’s counter claims. This news was first reported by Inman. Epique Realty did not immediately returned HousingWire’s request for comment. Related More: Epique Realty

items.title: Mortgage applications rise 6.1% even as 30-year hits 7.38%
items.description: Mortgage applications increased 6.1% from one week earlier, according to data from the Mortgage Bankers Association’s (MBA) weekly mortgage applications survey for the week ending November 20, 2026. On an unadjusted basis, the Index increased 3% compared with the previous week . The refinance index increased 1% from the previous week and was 51% lower than the same week one year ago. The seasonally adjusted purchase index increased 10% from one week earlier. The unadjusted purchase index increased 5% compared with the previous week and was 16% lower than the same week one year ago. “ Mortgage rates moved higher, with the 30-year fixed rate rising to 7.38%, its highest level in five weeks. While mortgage rates increased slightly on a weekly average basis, rates declined over the course of the week, which likely spurred purchase application activity,” said Joel Kan, CMB, MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist. “Purchase applications reached their strongest weekly pace since September but remained well behind last year’s pace." Kan added that a larger share of borrowers gravitated to ARM loans . The ARM share of activity accounted for 11.5% of applications, the highest share in more than a year, Kan noted. "At 6.39%, the ARM mortgage rate was nearly a full percentage lower than the 30-year fixed rate last week. Refinance activity was flat over the week with conventional applications showing a small increase while VA refinances dropped more than 11%," he said. The refinance share of mortgage activity decreased to 40.1% of total applications from 41.1% the previous week. The adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) share of activity increased to 11.5% of total applications. By product, the Federal Housing Administration ( FHA ) share of total applications decreased to 15.9% from 16.1% the week prior. The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs ( VA ) share decreased to 12.4% from 12.8% the week prior. The U.S. Department of Agriculture ( USDA ) share of total applications remained unchanged at 0.5% from the week prior. The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances ($832,750 or less) increased to 7.38% from 7.35%. Meanwhile, the average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with jumbo loan balances decreased to 7.29% from 7.31%. The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages backed by the FHA decreased to 7.05% from 7.06% while rates for 15-year fixed-rate mortgages increased to 6.79% from 6.64%. The average contract interest rate for 5/1 ARMs slightly increased to 6.39% from 6.38%. items.title: Simon Sues To Evict José Andrés-Affiliated Restaurant Over $2M In Unpaid Rent
items.description: Less than a year after a restaurant connected to celebrity chef and World Central Kitchen founder José Andrés debuted in Silicon Valley , the nation’s largest mall property management company is looking to take back the keys. Wikimedia Commons/Suiren2022 Stanford Shopping Center in Palo Alto, California Simon Property Group filed an unlawful detainer complaint Nov. 17, seeking to evict the upscale Eastern Mediterranean eatery Zaytinya from Stanford Shopping Center in Palo Alto , California, over nearly $2M in allegedly unpaid rent and other charges, the Palo Alto Daily Post reported . The lawsuit names restaurant leaseholder Mezze South Bay LLC and lease guarantor Think Food Group LLC as defendants. The latter operates under the José Andrés Group banner, with the chef serving as its founder and executive chairman. The Indianapolis-based REIT is seeking to terminate its 10-year lease with the entities behind the restaurant, Mezze South Bay LLC and Think Food Group LLC, and recover possession of the space . The lease called for initial monthly payments of $96,834, with additional rent tied to restaurant sales at initial rates from 13.625% to 21.5%, according to the San Francisco Chronicle . Simon is also seeking more than $3K in daily damages beginning Dec. 1 if the tenants remain in the space. items.title: The Lab Markets Next Door: Vacant Buildings Slowly Leasing Up In Watertown, Somerville
items.description: When the life sciences boom exploded out from the industry hub of Cambridge during the pandemic era, many developers bet the ripple effects would lead companies to expand in the neighboring cities of Watertown and Somerville. Some of those bets failed, as speculative lab projects delivered into a biotech market that was much slower than when they began construction, and vacancy rates in both cities rose above 50%. But a pickup in leasing activity this year has brought positive signs for Watertown and Somerville , even as vacancy remains high and developers face financial distress. Google Maps Ownership of the lab building at 808 Windsor St. in Somerville transferred to its lender in September. Researchers and landlords voiced optimism about both cities, but they said they are on different paths: The already established hub of Watertown is becoming a core market for the life sciences sector, whereas the newly developed cluster in Somerville still has a long road to recovery ahead. "Even though they're both next to Cambridge, I think just the makeup of the submarkets is so different," Cushman & Wakefield Research Manager Riley McMullan said. "Somerville, just as a life science market, is so new," she added. "In light of the demand dynamics changing, not seeing that leasing, not seeing those buildings really get leased up, that really affects the standing of Somerville as an ecosystem." Of the 2.4M SF of lab space in Somerville, all but 34K SF has been built since 2021, according to Cushman & Wakefield data. The market’s vacancy rate peaked at 75.6% last year, Cushman found, but a series of big leases this year has reduced it to 55.8%. Watertown is an older life sciences market, with 870K SF of its 3.4M SF of inventory built before 2021, according to Cushman. The city’s lab vacancy peaked at 52.4% in 2024 and is now down to 44%. "I think the reality is Watertown really got over that hump before the downturn," Davis Cos . Vice President of Asset Management Jon Needham said. "This is a story of Watertown being a primary market, and now you're seeing the primary markets outperform all other markets." An Established Market Early in the life sciences boom, Watertown had established itself as a major player, having a slightly older stock of life sciences buildings that would go on to fill the needs of biotech companies that had been priced out of Kendall Square and Boston. Needham referred to the area as the "Goldilocks zone," being in the perfect spot between suburban commuters and the major lab hubs in Kendall Square and Boston. "Watertown was a market that really wasn't a market going back — from a biotech standpoint — to 2012 to 2013, and then it really started building up as that overflow from Cambridge came out," Needham said. Many of the city’s life sciences buildings line the Arsenal Street corridor, with large developers including Davis Cos., Boylston Properties and Alexandria Real Estate Equities making big bets in the area — developing millions of square feet over several years. Through the first nine months of this year, the city secured 146K SF in life sciences leases from small to midsized biotech companies that are most active in the market, Cushman & Wakefield found. The biotech company joined Mariana Oncology, Vigil Therapeutics and Remix Therapeutics. In September, Google signed a 35K SF lease at Alexandria's 200 Talcott Ave. property, which is part of its 1.2M SF Arsenal on the Charles campus, the Boston Business Journal reported . The tech giant took space formerly occupied by Werewolf Therapeutics, which moved out after a merger. Alexandria also secured three biotech leases at the property in July: Ethyreal Bio, Olema Oncology and X4 Pharmaceuticals. Availability is still high for the market that once boasted a 2.9% vacancy rate, but the city's ability to adapt to the changing market fundamentals has helped in its recovery compared to other submarkets, Needham said. Davis and partner Boston Development Group broke ground speculatively in 2021 on 66 Galen St., a 224K SF life sciences building, and opened it in 2023. The project has since reached 95% leased, Needham said. The property is in the heart of Watertown Square and has secured leases from biotech flexible lab operator Labshares, which took 58K SF in 2025, and biotech entrepreneur Greg Verdine, who signed a 120K SF lease in 2024 for two of his startups. "I certainly believe that Watertown is doing very well and offers product that is a little bit different than other submarkets, and whether it's differentiated in quality or whether it's differentiated in the ability to put these alternative uses on the ground floor and have a mixed-use tenancy," Needham said. JLL Boston Research Director Mark Bruso told Bisnow in July that Watertown had become the region’s No. 2 life sciences cluster behind Cambridge. "Watertown has quickly grown to be the second-largest lab market, and there’s been, I think, a good amount of activity, specifically in the eastern east side of Watertown near Arsenal," he said. "You can make an argument that Watertown has been more active than the Seaport in the last six months." items.title: Patron Makes £250M Affordable Housing Push As Investors Warm To Sector
items.description: Unsplash/James Feaver Patron Capital and Hyde have formed a joint venture targeting more than £250M of investment in affordable housing, creating a new route for housebuilders to sell homes outside traditional Section 106 agreements. The partnership will work directly with developers across England to acquire new-build properties for shared ownership, social rent and affordable rent, with Persimmon the first housebuilder to join the programme. The venture is already deploying capital, with hundreds of homes secured and plans to build a national acquisition pipeline across multiple developers and schemes. The partners said the model would provide housebuilders with an additional source of demand and a more flexible route to deliver affordable housing, while bringing institutional investment into a sector traditionally reliant on public funding and housing association balance sheets. The investment will focus on two- and three-bedroom family homes aimed at first-time buyers, including properties in locations where affordable housing has previously been less widely available. Hyde and Patron will provide equity to acquire the properties, with Hyde's specialist investment management business, Hyde Capital Partners, formerly Pinnacle Investments, having structured the partnership and leading the acquisition programme. "Our ambition is to create long-term partnerships with housebuilders that bring more institutional investment into affordable housing. Working across multiple developments, we can offer a flexible, reliable source of capital that helps support future housing delivery," Hyde Capital Partners Managing Director Chris Turnbull said in a statement. Patron Capital Managing Director Keith Breslauer said he believes institutional capital could play a key role in meeting demand for affordable homes when deployed “through the right structures and with the right partners." "Our partnership with Patron brings its residential investment expertise together with Hyde's national housing platform. This in turn serves our charitable purpose, with any surpluses we generate reinvested in our homes and the communities we serve," Hyde Group Chief Executive Andy Hulme added. Hyde is a group led by a not-for-profit housing association, which owns or manages about 130,000 homes, making it one of the largest housing providers in the country. It also provides neighbourhood services to more than 350,000 homes across the UK. Investors including Brookfield and Sixth Street have also moved into the affordable housing sector this year, following in the footsteps of private equity early movers like Blackstone and Man Group. items.title: Multifamily Debt Brokerage Meridian Capital Group Hit With Ransomware Hack
items.description: Meridian Capital Group , one of the country’s largest multifamily debt brokerages, was hacked by a high-profile group with ties to Russia. Unsplash/Julio Lopez Qilin , a ransomware-as-a-service group, said in a Nov. 17 post on its website that it had breached Meridian Capital Group’s cybersecurity, The Real Deal reported . The firm confirmed the hack in a statement to the outlet. “Meridian Capital Group was one of dozens of companies targeted recently,” a spokesperson said. “Upon detecting an intrusion, we activated our cybersecurity response plan and are engaging with law enforcement and our key counterparties and stakeholders. The privacy and security of data entrusted to us by our customers and employees is a top priority, and we will notify any affected parties as appropriate.” Meridian Capital Group didn’t respond to Bisnow ’s request for comment Wednesday morning. The debt firm is one of the biggest players in the agency space, arranging loans for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac . It was also previously part of a partnership with Barings called NewPoint Real Estate Capital that Meridian sold last year . Qilin was first active in 2022, and cybersecurity experts say its attacks likely originate from Russia. The group provides tools to hackers to initiate ransomware attacks in exchange for a piece of the earnings. The group, which typically uses phishing emails to gain control over systems, has previously hacked the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, the UK’s National Health Service, the Japanese brewer Asahi and the Chinese car parts manufacturer Yanfen, TRD reported. Qilin typically threatens to leak the data it is holding unless it is paid, with ransoms ranging from $50K to $800K in 2023, according to cybersecurity firm Group-IB, TRD reported. The hack potentially could have compromised sensitive or confidential client data. Ransomware attacks have long plagued the corporate world, but the recent breach comes at a time when a wide range of digital systems around the country — from air traffic control to Microsoft Outlook — are facing widespread technical challenges that are raising questions about the resilience of the systems that underpin daily and economic life. Qilin and another hacker group called ShinyHunters also claimed responsibility for a breach of Cushman & Wakefield systems that led to a class-action lawsuit from customers of the brokerage in May. Turner Construction also disclosed in August that it was hit with a data breach that gave hackers access to military project files, nondisclosure agreements and personal information. The construction firm was targeted by a different ransomware group called Payout Kings that claimed responsibility for the hack and said it collected 27.2 terabytes' worth of data. items.description: Optimus Properties Buys South Pasadena Mixed-Use Asset for $6.45M Optimus Properties LLC has acquired a two-building, 17,053-square-foot mixed-use property in downtown South Pasadena for $6.45 million. The historic buildings, located at 1500 and 1508 Mission St., were constructed in 1923 and 1908, respectively. The property contains 12,887 square feet of ground-floor retail space across six suites along with eight apartment units. Situated on a 23,253-square-foot lot with 23 parking spaces, the buildings occupy roughly half a block along South Pasadena’s primary retail corridor and sits steps from the Metro A Line station at Mission and Meridian. Optimus has extended the lease of longtime tenant Two Kids Coffee through 2031 and signed a new five-year lease with Nott & Associates, a design-build firm that has occupied space at the property for nearly 30 years. Perilla L.A., chef Jihee Kim’s Korean banchan shop, will open its second location at 1504 Mission St. The acquisition reflects a shift in Optimus’ investment strategy as the firm redirects capital away from the City of Los Angeles into other California communities. The proposed 96,600-square-foot hotel will occupy a portion of the existing parking area at 2111 E. Highland Ave., just south of Camelback Road. Tucson-based Holualoa acquired the approximately 12-acre property, formerly known as Park One, in December 2021. In 2025, the firm completed a $10 million renovation of the two-building, 209,000-square-foot office complex that included modernized office suites, upgraded lobbies and tenant amenities, a lakeside boardwalk, a putting green and outdoor recreational facilities. The project expands Holualoa’s Phoenix-area hospitality portfolio, which includes the 277-room, dual-branded AC Hotel and Element development at Norterra and a 240-room dual-branded Marriott property scheduled to open at CityNorth in December. Preliminary plans were filed with the City of Phoenix in October, with pre-development activities expected to conclude in mid-2027. items.title: CoStar photographers say quotas rose, now some want to unionize
items.description: Earlier this fall, CoStar Group hosted its first Global Photography Conference in Richmond, Virginia. The event, which was held at the firm’s new Foundry Park campus, was largely lauded as a success by CoStar and even members of its photography team . CoStar CEO Andy Florance, also celebrated what appeared to be a successful event, writing in a post on LinkedIn that the team set the standard “for future collaboration as they shared techniques, tested new ideas and innovated what's next for visual storytelling in real estate.” “I’m excited to see what they continue to build, one image at a time,” Florance, a HousingWire Vanguard , added. But under the surface, sources that spoke with HousingWire said that things within the listing portal giant’s photography team are not as hunky-dory as the social media posts paint them out to be. Over the past few weeks HousingWire has spoken with several sources within CoStar about a recent unionization effort among the company’s architectural photographers, which were the photographers behind the content used for the Homes.com Neighborhood Guides . The sources, who asked for anonymity due to fear of retribution, claim that the workload for architectural photographers is “unmanageable” and “impossible to complete within the working hours.” In 2025, CoStar raised daily quotas for architectural photographers, which was followed by a move this September to lower the point value of assignments, which means, according to the sources, that photographers have to do more work each day to meet their minimum quotas. Rising workloads Last year, work quotas were raised from 0.8 per day to 1.0 per day and the point value of different tiers was dropped from 1 point to 0.75 point for Diamond, from 0.75 point to 0.50 point for Platinum and from 0.50 point to 0.25 point for Gold. This means that, in the past, photographers could complete one Diamond project and meet their daily quota, but now they have to do one Diamond project and one Gold project to meet quota. Sources also claimed that there is no work-life balance as they sometimes have to drive over an hour to go to and from appointments and that it takes well over an hour to upload the images captured that day. However, sources did note that CoStar has outsourced the photo editing work to help offset some of these issues, which the company confirmed. Challenges are compounded by layoffs, sources say Despite this shift in responsibilities, the sources said all of these challenges have been compounded by layoffs creating shortages of architectural photographers across the country. Sources said that this sometimes requires them to travel far outside their normal service areas further increasing drive times. “Not only did they bump up the daily requirement by 25%, they also scrapped any sort of flexible scheduling. Now every single photographer is expected to be on-call 12 hours a day, Monday through Friday. No exceptions. This change came [out of] nowhere,” a user named richmondrefugee posted in a subreddit called r/RealEstatePhotography. “And if that wasn’t enough, today they let go of two dozen folks — just like that. It’s been a mess, y’all.” In addition to this, the sources said they are concerned for their job security as the company continues to cut the architectural photography staff while hiring residential photographers. This is a more entry-level position at CoStar and as such these photographers are compensated at a lower rate. Sources within the company said that these other photographers were brought in to do Matterports , but are being sent out to do assignments that architectural photographers have done in the past. “They had me train my replacement! I was getting paid six figures and one day they asked me to train this "Matterport Photographer," making $40K. So I spent the week with him training. One day I was at his trunk when he was getting his Matterport and saw his Costar bag with all the same gear as me. I said why are they giving a Matterport photographer over 10K in camera equipment. A month later I was gone and they have him doing my job,” KeepitMelloOoW posted in the r/RealEstatePhotogrpahy subreddit. The decision to unionize Sources told HousingWire that these concerns about job security, work load and work-life balance are what prompted the architectural photography team to explore the idea of unionizing by joining the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW). This resulted in a link to an IBEW unionization interest form being circulated within CoStar. Unsurprisingly, the link caught the attention of CoStar management. In response to the link, Lisa Ruggles, CoStar’s senior vice president of global operations sent an email to all of the firm’s photographers that was obtained by HousingWire and verified by CoStar, in which she said that CoStar was “was surprised to hear of an anonymous email afterward urging Architectural Photographers to join the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers,” in light of the success of the Global Photography Conference. According to the email, “media shoots” are the “top priority” for the firm’s architectural photography team and that the point values for assignment changed due to the outsourcing of editing and post-production of images. “Photo retouching now goes to a dedicated resource, while Matterport and floor-plan uploads are automated —removing tasks photographers once handled. We must use new technology to compete. A union cannot change the work our customers demand or our business requires,” Ruggles wrote. Ruggles also noted that the change in point values also helped level the playing field and make sure all photographers from across the company were completing the same level of work. items.title: Foreign Buyers Pull Back From U.S., but Canadian Snowbirds Widen Their Lead
items.description: Foreign homebuyers retreated from the U.S. housing market this fall, driven by an exodus of European shoppers. This shift helped Canadians cement their dominance. Between July and September 2026, global house hunters accounted for 1.3% of traffic on Realtor.com® , down from 1.5% a year ago, according to the latest quarterly International Demand report released on Wednesday. Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu attributes the broader slowdown to a combination of factors, including geopolitical uncertainty, shifting trade policies, and persistent inflation challenges. Yet against that downturn, Canada's share of demand has expanded, climbing to 35.9% of overall international traffic and reinforcing its hold on the top spot among foreign buyers. This development marks a turnaround from a year ago, when Canadian interest in U.S. real estate dipped to 32.3% amid President Donald Trump 's aggressive tariff policies , which defined the beginning of his second term in office. Sun-soaked Florida remains the premier destination for Canadian snowbirds escaping freezing Northern winters, commanding nearly 29% of Canada's search traffic. Meanwhile, Texas edged past California as the second-most popular market for Canadians, drawing 8.8% of traffic compared with the Golden State's 8.6%. "I’m seeing continued interest from Canadian buyers in Southern California," Daniel Zakharia , an agent with Douglas Elliman Beverly Hills , tells Realtor.com. "While political and economic uncertainty prompted some Canadian homeowners to reconsider their U.S. real estate holdings in 2025, particularly in traditional snowbird markets such as Palm Springs, recent reporting following the November midterm elections suggests that some Canadians are reconsidering their decisions to sell or stay away." Zakharia, himself a Canadian transplant, notes that California’s climate, lifestyle, and global connectivity remain fundamental attractions for Canadian buyers, who are most often drawn to turnkey properties with minimal maintenance, added privacy, security, and resort-style amenities. Loading... Canadians are flocking to Big Sky Country The third-quarter 2026 data also highlights Montana 's growing appeal, with the mountain state drawing 2% of Canadian search demand, up from 1.3% in 2019. By comparison, Montana accounted for just 1.2% of overall international traffic during the same period. "My experience has been that, typically, the Canadian buyers buy in the northern sections of Montana, as it has greater proximity to the border," Chase Heiland , real estate broker with Keller Williams Montana Realty , tells Realtor.com. Echoing Xu, Heiland maintains that economic uncertainty surrounding tariffs on imports, elevated consumer prices, and an unfavorable exchange rate for the Canadian dollar are keeping many prospective buyers on sidelines. Loading... However, those who do buy are taking a long-term view. Heiland recently helped Canadians moving to Bozeman, MT , for a job opportunity to purchase a home in the area. "We walked through the pros and cons of single-family homes versus townhomes versus condos," he recounts. "They opted for a single-family home to best preserve its value moving forward, as well as being a good long-term investment into Bozeman and Montana as a whole." Despite cooling international demand nationwide, Heiland notes that he has worked with more overseas buyers this year than at any other point in his career. "Montana and Bozeman are very much on the map in a way they weren't before," says the agent. "I've had clients not only from Canada this year, but [also] from Russia, Mexico, and Pakistan. They all gravitated toward single-family homes in the city center, with access to everything Bozeman offers and easy access to the area's recreation." Loading... Montana drew 2% of Canadian home search demand this fall, up from 1.3% in 2019. Getty Images Top Canadian enclaves At the metro level, Cape Coral, FL , retained its strong pull among Northern neighbors, with roughly 66% of its international traffic coming from Canada in the third quarter, up 8.9 percentage points from a year ago for the largest annual gain among major markets. Known as "the Venice of America," Cape Coral boasts over 400 miles of canals, many of them with golf course access, along with dozens of parks and family attractions. Naples, FL , saw 65.4% of its foreign traffic coming from Canada in the third quarter, followed by Phoenix (62.6%) and North Port, FL (61.4%). Loading... Cape Coral, FL, is the most popular U.S. metro among Canadians, with nearly 66% of international traffic coming from Canada. Europeans accounted for just under a quarter (24.5%) of all international homebuyers this fall, the lowest level since 2019, according to the quarterly data. U.K. house hunters made up 6.2% of foreign traffic, followed by Germany at 3.7%, both marking seven-year lows for the third quarter. "The decline coincides with weaker European travel to the U.S. , suggesting that European interest in U.S. homes may be cooling alongside interest in visiting," says Xu. However, Zakharia points out that international buyer behavior is not uniform, and that it is important to distinguish between discretionary second-home purchases and those driven by professional or business opportunities.
